papers.title: Computational Compound Prioritization Strategy Incorporating Docking Variability and Interaction Energies Identifies Putative LRH-1 Binders
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
papers.abs: Compound ranking in structure-based computer-aided drug discovery notoriously yields highly ranked false positives due to sampling and, more frequently, scoring errors. We developed a compound prioritization strategy that utilizes sampled docked poses from complementary docking approaches, i.e., targeted physics-based docking and blind docking with a generative model, into multiple conformations of the target protein to train two multilayer perceptron (MLP) models. The MLPs predict binders or activators at the orthosteric ligand-binding pocket of the nuclear receptor Liver Receptor Homologue-1 (LRH-1, NR5A2). Our approach circumvents the reliance on a single docked pose for scoring compounds or individual scoring metrics for compound ranking. In an out-of-distribution compound set, we observed that the MLPs identified compounds that are chemically dissimilar from those in the training set and are sensitive to single scaffold modifications, making the MLPs potential tools for lead optimization. We applied the MLPs on a pilot study prospective drug discovery campaign, which resulted in the identification of four putative LRH-1 binders. We found that a combination of scoring and prediction metrics enriches for hit compounds across library sizes. In all, this work presents a method to leverage structural and experimental data to aid drug discovery for a challenging protein target.

papers.title: Resolving kinetics of halide separation in perovskites by polaron-based lattice model and in situ X-ray diffraction
papers.jname: npj Computational Materials
papers.abs: Light-induced phase separation (LIPS) in mixed lead-halide perovskites is one of the major obstacles to high-efficiency perovskite-based tandem solar cells, yet the mechanisms that govern it remain unclear. Using in situ X-ray diffraction on MAPbBr 1.8 I 1.2 , we track coexisting phases through their lattice parameters and observe the same kinetics across all samples: phase separation sets in only after a delay, with an iodide-rich phase appearing abruptly at near-pure composition while the residual mixed phase drifts gradually towards bromide. To capture this behaviour, we extend the Kawasaki Hamiltonian, adding separate polaron-induced stress terms for electrons and holes, and evolve the halide lattice by Monte Carlo simulation. The model reproduces both the delay and the asymmetry, neither of which follows from standard Cahn-Hilliard kinetics. Within the model, the stronger coupling of electron polarons in bromide-rich regions dominates the driving force, pointing to electron-phonon coupling as a lever for suppressing LIPS.

papers.title: Optical Absorption and Exciton Dispersion of Bulk Corrugated g-C3N4
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Graphitic carbon nitride (g-C3N4) is a promising layered metal-free photocatalyst whose optical properties are strongly affected by structural corrugation induced by nitrogen lone-pair repulsion. However, calculations for the bulk have largely focused on the ideal planar structure. Here, we investigate the structural, electronic, and excitonic properties of corrugated bulk g-C3N4 using density functional theory, many-body perturbation theory, and the Bethe–Salpeter equation. The absorption spectrum is dominated by bound excitons below the quasiparticle gap, with the first bright exciton at 2.75 eV (dark in the ideal flat structure) in good agreement with experiment. Bulk excitons arise from symmetric and antisymmetric combinations of monolayer excitations mixed by interlayer hopping, leading to a Davydov splitting and to states with mixed Frenkel and charge-transfer character. Their bandwidths are only a few to a few tens of meV, indicating inefficient exciton propagation both in-plane and out-of-plane.

papers.title: Understanding the Surface and Interfacial Structure of N -Heterocyclic Carbenes on Ruthenium Substrates: An X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopic Approach
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: N-Heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs) are exceptional σ-donors and bind strongly to a wide variety of transition metals. Their unique binding properties have expanded the potential applications of NHCs to area-selective atomic layer deposition (AS-ALD) for microelectronics fabrication. This new application area requires a deeper understanding of the NHC-to-metal interaction beyond the scale of small molecule NHC–metal complexes. Various surface characterization techniques have been applied to study the NHC-deposited metal surfaces, but to date, most studies have been limited to NHCs deposited on single crystals. Ru is an appealing material in the semiconductor industry because of its moderate resistivity and low electromigration rate. There remains a lack of understanding regarding the surface chemistry of NHCs on Ru metal, with the knowledge gained from NHCs on single crystals not necessarily transferable to NHCs on the polycrystalline substrates encountered in microelectronic devices. To bridge this gap, we report herein an in-depth X-ray photoelectron spectroscopic investigation into the interactions between NHCs and polycrystalline Ru surfaces. Two NHC derivatives with different wingtip and backbone groups were employed. Using different incident energies providing varied penetration depths, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopic measurements were conducted to provide insight into how changes in the NHC structure impact the surface coverage density, molecule-to-metal charge transfer, and the ability to protect Ru surfaces.

papers.title: Light-Controlled Electrostatics at Redox-Active Metal–Organic Framework Heterointerfaces
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Interfacial electrostatics are central to charge separation, catalysis, sensing, energy conversion, and electronic transport, but the built-in potential of heterojunctions is generally considered fixed by the constituent materials. Here we show that redox-active metal–organic framework (MOF) heterointerfaces enable reversible optical control over the junction electrostatics. A heterostructured thin film assembled from n-type Cu-BHT (BHT = benzenehexathiol) and p-type Cu-ADA (ADA = azobenzenedicarboxylate) exhibits pronounced current rectification together with a light-induced increase in the cut-in voltage by ∼0.9 V. Spectroscopic measurements identify Cu(I) centers and sulfur radical anions as photoactive redox sites. Combined electrical measurements and density functional theory calculations reveal substantial interfacial charge reconstruction and a Type-I band alignment that confines photogenerated holes near the junction. This charge accumulation expands the depletion region and increases the built-in potential, as corroborated by the capacitance–voltage measurements. Our findings establish MOF heterojunctions as chemically programmable platforms for dynamic control of interfacial electrostatics and adaptive optoelectronic functionality.

papers.title: Hydrogen-Bond-Induced Dual Structural Response in Amide-Functionalized Self-Assembled Monolayers
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Internal functionalization can reorganize intermolecular interactions across a self-assembled monolayer (SAM), yet its depth-dependent consequences remain poorly understood. Here, molecular dynamics simulations and vibrational sum-frequency generation (VSFG) spectroscopy reveal a dual structural response in N-(2-mercaptoethyl)heptanamide SAMs on Au(111). A persistent intermolecular hydrogen-bonding network suppresses conformational fluctuations between the Au–S interface and the amide plane. Above this plane, however, the larger volume of the amide increases alkyl-chain separation, weakens van der Waals coupling, and enhances conformational flexibility with temperature. Thus, a hydrogen-bond-stabilized, solid-like lower region coexists with a weakly coupled, liquid-like upper region. Simulated VSFG spectra reproduce the observed terminal CH3 stretching-mode intensities, including the enhanced asymmetric response. This response occurs without a correspondingly large average methyl tilt angle because inequivalent molecular environments produce broad, heterogeneous orientation distributions. Consequently, the conventional assignment of a single methyl tilt angle from VSFG intensity ratio breaks down for internally functionalized SAMs.

papers.title: Controlled Growth and Disorder Mitigation of GaAs1– x Sb x /InAs Core–Shell Quantum Wires
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: We report the growth and transport properties of GaAs1–xSbx/InAs core–shell nanowires. Compared with the well-studied GaAs-InAs system, incorporating Sb substantially reduces the lattice mismatch between the core and shell. Accordingly, both the nanowire crystal quality and device performance improved significantly. Increasing x from 0.15 to 0.35, the density of crystalline defects, such as stacking faults in the InAs shell, decreases by half. Moreover, the field-effect mobility increases from 3850 cm2/(V s) to 4800 cm2/(V s), consistent with the reduction of the lattice mismatch. The incorporation of Sb makes the nanowire easier to pinch off via the gate voltage, enhancing the electric field tunability over the nanowire. Magneto-conductance measurements reveal Aharonov-Bohm-like oscillations, suggesting a phase-coherent tubular InAs shell. Our results identify lattice mismatch as a critical disorder source in core–shell nanowires and provide a practical route toward low-disorder core–shell quantum devices.

papers.title: Growth Temperature of Integrated 2D SnS Microrods with Sulfur Vacancies Enabling Ultrahigh Power Na-Ion Microbatteries
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: “Microbatteries” are known to be the key to device miniaturization, but the practicality associated with one such domain of SnS thin films in Na-ion microbatteries (Na-μBs) is limited by slow Na+ kinetics and cycling-induced pulverization. These issues are strongly affected by microstructure, crystallinity, and interface quality, which can be tuned through growth temperature; however, their correlation with electrochemical performance remains unclear. Herein, SnS thin films with a thickness of 86.76 ± 4 nm were prepared via hydrothermal-assisted thermal evaporation at varying growth substrate temperatures. The optimal film growth occurs at 200 °C under sulfur-deficient conditions, yielding a high areal discharge capacity of 55 μAh/cm2 at a high current density of 200 μA/cm2 and remarkable retention of 88.6% over 150 cycles. The CV and DFT analyses reveal the capacitive–diffusive kinetics and charge localization around sulfur in SnS, facilitating Na–S bonds in conversion alloying reactions. Furthermore, demonstrations of powering LEDs highlight the practical applicability of SnS thin films as anodes in Na-μBs.

papers.title: Beyond Single-Ligand Superhalogen Coordination: Unveiling the d -Orbital Contribution as the Electronic Origin in Heteroleptic Silver-Based Hyperhalogens
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Traditional hyperhalogen design relies heavily on homoleptic coordination between a metal center and superhalogen ligands, a constraint that fundamentally limits structural diversity in this field. Here, we report a new class of heteroleptic hyperhalogens, [Ag(BO2)(B2O4)]−, [Ag2(BO2)(B2O4)]−, and [Ag2(BO2)(B3O6)]−, which were synthesized in the gas phase and characterized by time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometry and quantum chemical calculations. Experimental results show that precise control over the spectral conditions enables the selective synthesis of these clusters. Theoretical calculations demonstrate that the heteroleptic design endows the clusters with exceptional hyperhalogen properties. Electronic structure analysis further reveals a positive correlation between hyperhalogen behavior and the d-orbital contribution from the Ag atoms to the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO). This discovery suggests that synergistic interactions between different superhalogen moieties could have broad applicability in synthetic design, offering new perspectives on the coordination chemistry of superatomic clusters and opening a transformative avenue for hyperhalogen research.

papers.title: A Comparative Study of Coherent and Fluorescence-Detected 2D Electronic Spectroscopies of a Multichromophore Photosynthetic System
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Coherent two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy (C-2DES) is a powerful tool for resolving excitonic structure and dynamics in light-harvesting complexes with dense energy-level manifolds. In contrast, action-detected 2DES (A-2DES) has seen limited use on such systems, and its capacity to reveal electronic structure and dynamics remains unclear. Here we compare C-2DES and fluorescence-detected 2DES (F-2DES) on the major plant light-harvesting complex (LHCII) at 78 K. C-2DES clearly resolves excitonic features and their spectral evolution, mapping energy-transfer pathways. F-2DES shows strong cross-peaks, but these are largely time-invariant and dominated by incoherent mixing, obscuring the dynamics. C-2DES is therefore preferred for resolving ultrafast energy transfer in light-harvesting complexes and other large interacting molecular networks. Combined, the two measurements place a lower bound on the size of the chromophore domain contributing to incoherent mixing: C-2DES resolves the population-transfer dynamics, while their absence above the F-2DES noise floor constrains the minimum size of the annihilation domain through the combinatorial model. We obtain lower limits of 12 and 9 chromophores at the analyzed peaks, consistent with an energy-transfer domain extending over a substantial fraction of the LHCII trimer.
papers.zh: 多发色团光合作用系统相干和荧光检测2D电子光谱的比较研究

papers.title: One Interface, Two Driving Forces: Channel-Resolved Ultrafast Spectroscopy Separates Charge-Transfer Rate from Charge-Generation Yield in PTO2:IT-4F Organic Solar Cells
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Efficient charge transfer at near-zero frontier-orbital offset is established; whether a fast transfer rate guarantees a high charge-generation yield is not. We examine this in PTO2:IT-4F (PCE 14.7%), whose HOMO (∼0.07 eV) and LUMO (∼0.52 eV) offsets are strongly asymmetric: 720 nm excitation opens only the near-zero-offset hole channel, whereas 530 nm excitation also opens the conventional-offset electron channel at the same junction. At 720 nm, a PTO2 hole-polaron bleach at 550 nm, free of acceptor features, reports hole transfer directly. Global target analysis in which all IT-4F excitons share one spectrum, requiring no extinction coefficients, shows that only about 45% of the excitons transfer in 0.57 ps; the rest transfer in 4.5 ps after diffusing to an interface, for a total injection yield of at least 60%. The yield is limited downstream: about 42% of the bound pairs recombine geminately (τ ≈ 140 ps). At 530 nm, energy transfer and direct electron-transfer quench PTO2 excitons within the instrument response in similar proportions (energy transfer ≈0.5, electron transfer ≈0.5). A delayed rise assigned to long-range separation persists in PTO2:IT-4F but is nearly absent in PTO2:PC71BM despite its larger HOMO offset, pointing to the donor/acceptor pair rather than energetic alignment as the origin of the high efficiency.

papers.title: Abnormal Increase in Thermal Diffusivity of Lignin-Based Carbon Fibers during Vacuum Exposure
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Vacuum generally suppresses gaseous heat conduction without altering intrinsic transport of solid materials. Here we report an unexpected, time-dependent increase in thermal diffusivity (α) of lignin-based carbon fibers (CFs) during vacuum exposure. At <0.08 Pa, α increases by up to ∼95% and approaches saturation, while its electrical resistance (R) shows smaller, condition-dependent changes. After ∼16 h of air re-exposure, α partially or nearly fully recovers, while R responds less consistently, demonstrating strong dependence on exposure history. Across the vacuum systems examined, the α increase diminishes as vacuum pressure rises from <0.08 to 2.13 Pa, whereas a moderate temperature rise (∼50 K) accelerates the evolution of the α increase under ∼0.21 Pa vacuum. Laser-power-normalized Raman intensities increase during air re-exposure without significant D- or G-band shifts, providing indirect evidence of reversible near-surface-state evolution rather than restructuring of the carbon framework. Atomistic simulations show that adsorbed water shortens acoustic phonon lifetimes and suppresses in-plane thermal transport. These results support vacuum-induced desorption of near-surface adsorbates as reducing phonon scattering and increasing α, as there is negligible change in volumetric heat capacity. Removal of humidity-assisted charge-transport pathways may also contribute to the increase in R observed in some sequences. It is concluded that the exposure history is an important factor in thermal and electrical measurements of carbon fibers under vacuum.
papers.zh: 木质素基碳纤维在真空暴露过程中的热扩散率异常增加

papers.title: Near-Thermoneutral Hydrogen Adsorption at Sulfur Dangling-Bond Sites of an Experimentally Observed MoS2 Grain Boundary
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Grain boundaries (GBs) in monolayer 1H-MoS2 can provide favorable hydrogen-adsorption sites relevant to the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), but the atomistic origin of this behavior remains unclear for experimentally realized boundary structures. Here, spin-polarized density functional theory calculations are performed to investigate an experimentally observed ∼18° MoS2 GB containing an apparently periodic sequence of five-, seven-, and four-membered rings, i.e., 5–7–4 GB motif. Four local configurations (α1, α2, β1, and β2) are examined as candidate structures of the 5–7–4 GB motif. The β-oriented supercell exhibits a lower average GB formation energy (11.02 eV nm–1) than the α-oriented supercell (12.86 eV nm–1), while β1 most closely reproduces the experimentally inferred bond connectivity. GB reconstruction generates boundary-localized Mo 4d and S 3p states near the Fermi level. Among six distinct sulfur environments, the undercoordinated h2 (α1) and h4 (β1) sites exhibit near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption free energies of −0.20 and −0.05 eV, respectively. Occupied nonbonding states localized on these sulfur sites provide a plausible electronic origin for their favorable hydrogen adsorption thermodynamics.

papers.title: Tuning Magnetic Stability in Lanthanide Single-Atom Magnets on Defective Boron Nitride: From Intrinsic Protection to Field-Induced Spin-Lifetime Engineering
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: The pursuit of atomic-scale magnetic storage has driven intense research into lanthanide-based single-atom magnets (SAMs), where magnetic bistability and long magnetic relaxation times are essential for practical applications. However, a fundamental challenge is to achieve strong uniaxial magnetic anisotropy while simultaneously suppressing quantum tunneling of magnetization (QTM), since the former stabilizes the magnetization whereas the latter enables rapid relaxation and undermines magnetic memory. Here, we systematically investigate the magnetic stability and relaxation dynamics of Ho (4f10, J = 8) and Tb (4f8, J = 6) adatoms adsorbed on defective hexagonal boron nitride (Dh-BN) with C3v symmetry, using an integrated approach combining density functional theory (DFT+U+SOC) and model Hamiltonian analysis. Our results reveal that the interplay between total angular momentum J and crystal field symmetry dictates the intrinsic magnetic stability. For Ho@Dh-BN, C3v symmetry protects the degenerate |J = 8, mJ ≈ ±8⟩ ground states from QTM, as transverse crystal field terms (ΔmJ = ±3) cannot mix the |±8⟩ states. This yields a substantial effective reversal barrier of Urev = 28.72 meV and an Arrhenius magnetic lifetime of 1150 s at 12 K, demonstrating robust zero-field stability. In stark contrast, Tb@Dh-BN exhibits strong mixing of its |J = 6, mJ ≈ ±6⟩ ground states via QTM channels, resulting in a vanishing reversal barrier and no magnetic stability at zero field. Remarkably, applying an external magnetic field (B = 8 T) along the easy axis can restore the stability in the Tb system: the magnetic field lifts the ground-state degeneracy to suppress QTM by purifying the wave functions and forces magnetization reversal to proceed via multistep spin-flip pathways. This raises an effective barrier to Urev = 42.10 meV and extends the Arrhenius magnetic lifetime to 791 s at 18 K. Our work establishes two complementary design principles for achieving long spin lifetimes in lanthanide SAMs: intrinsic protection through favorable combinations of J and crystal field symmetry that inherently forbid QTM, and active field-induced stabilization that dynamically suppresses QTM in otherwise unstable systems. The findings provide a comprehensive microscopic understanding of magnetic relaxation in surface-supported lanthanide atoms and offer a clear theoretical roadmap for engineering electrically or magnetically addressable atomic-scale memory devices.

papers.title: Single-Atom-Intermediated Raman Activation (SAIRA) Mechanism on Pyridine-Adsorbed Au/g-C3N4 and Periodic Trends from a 30 d-Block Element Screening
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) on single-atom platforms offers a reproducible, hotspot-free sensing paradigm, yet its fundamental mechanism remains elusive. Herein, we present a comprehensive density functional theory (DFT) investigation into the “Single-Atom-Intermediated Raman Activation (SAIRA)” mechanism using a pyridine-adsorbed Au/g-C3N4 model. Ground-state electronic structure analyses reveal that the cavity-confined Au single atom acts as an indispensable polarization center that triggers strong orbital hybridization and interfacial charge transfer upon molecular adsorption. Consequently, the simulated static Raman activity yields a chemical enhancement factor about 1 order of magnitude higher than that of conventional Au20 clusters. Based on a model chemistry established through systematic benchmark evaluations of DFT functionals and basis sets, this protocol successfully captured experimental observations across various probe molecules. Importantly, extending this validated protocol to a two-dimensional descriptor map based on energetic and electronic parameters for 30 d-block elements reveals that the systems segregate into three distinct mechanistic domains, exhibiting pronounced interdomain variations in Raman enhancement. Furthermore, this 2D descriptor mapping demonstrates high robustness against alternative model chemistries. Ultimately, this work establishes electronic-level design principles not only for next-generation single-atom-based SERS technologies but also for the rational design of functional single-atom catalysts.

papers.title: Direct Observation of Crystal Structures and Raman Spectra during Photochemical Changes of Organic Charge-Transfer Complexes: Thermodynamic Aspect of Heavy Atom Effects
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: For insight into photochemical processes, it is required to observe structures and spectra with the corresponding thermodynamic functions and electronic states. We have compared the photochemical processes between MV[NiL2]2 (L = 1,3-dithole-2-selone-4,5-dithiolate, the selone derivative, or L = 1,3-dithiole-2-thione-4,5-dithiolate, the thione derivative), which exhibited sufficiently slow photochemical changes to observe them by various methods, to study heavy-atom effects on photoluminescence. X-ray single-crystal structural analyses, first-principles calculations, and Raman spectra indicated that, in both derivatives after cessation of photoirradiation, their molecular orbitals, charge distributions, and thermodynamic quantities remained changing for weeks to months. Triggered by a 532 nm laser, the selone derivative more efficiently emitted infrared light than did the thione derivative. Comparison between the two derivatives revealed structural and thermodynamic aspects of heavy-atom effects. The findings bridge macroscopic and microscopic viewpoints of photoinduced phenomena in materials, providing experimental grounds for theories.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Studies of Ester-Based Gemini Surfactant and Nitrogen-Doped Graphene Quantum Dot Coacervation and Its Application in Quercetin Detection
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: Coacervation is spontaneous phase separation into colloid-rich and dilute phases. Here, we report self-assembled luminescent coacervate droplets formed by mixing nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots (NGQDs) with an ester-based cationic gemini surfactant in water. Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) confirmed the formation of intrinsically fluorescent spherical droplets. Double-logarithmic plot analysis and Van’t Hoff thermodynamic studies revealed that the spontaneous formation of stable luminescent coacervate droplets is primarily driven by hydrogen bonding and van der Waals interactions. Fluorescence, UV–vis spectroscopy, lifetime measurements, and temperature-dependent Stern–Volmer studies showed that quercetin-induced fluorescence quenching of the coacervate droplets proceeds through a synergistic combination of static quenching, PET-mediated dynamic quenching, and the inner filter effect (IFE), providing a simple and selective fluorometric sensing approach. The sensor exhibited a linear response in the range of 5–50 μM, with detection limits of 5.7 nM in deionized (DI) water and 7.1 nM in tap water. The fluorescent probe effectively measured quercetin in biological samples (human serum, plasma, whole blood) and real samples (Java plum, tomato) with recovery rates ranging from 94.9% to 108.3%. This turn-off droplet-based platform provides a simple, rapid, and effective method for quercetin detection, demonstrating the potential of hybrid nanomaterials in advanced sensing applications.

papers.title: The Correlated States Theory of Nonpolar Solvation in Normal van der Waals Liquids
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: In the present work, we developed a new thermodynamic theory of solvation of nonpolar molecules in nonpolar van der Waals liquids, built as a limiting case of nonpolar solvation in polar liquid at the enthalpy/entropy convergence temperatures tending to infinity. Expressions for the full set of thermodynamic functions of solvation (ΔG, ΔH, ΔS, ΔCP), corrected for the Kuhn-like segment, were derived in closed analytical form and demonstrated a good match with the extended experimental data set for nonpolar solvation in own neat liquids (branched alkanes, linear alkanes/alkenes, aromatics). It was shown that the enthalpy–entropy compensation phenomenon, Trouton’s law, and zero transfer energy between different van der Waals liquids, known from previous empirical studies, stem as partial cases from the equations of the developed theory.

papers.title: Mechanism of Tau Diffusion along Microtubules
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: By one-dimensional diffusion, proteins can search biological polymers while remaining associated with them. Tau, an intrinsically disordered microtubule-associated protein, undergoes rapid diffusion along the microtubule (MT) lattice primarily through electrostatic interactions with tubulin C-terminal tails (CTTs), yet the molecular mechanism underlying this behavior has remained unresolved. Here, we performed coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to characterize the diffusion mechanism of full-length Tau at domain and subdomain resolution. We show that Tau diffusion emerges from the heterogeneous translational behaviors of multiple weakly coupled MT-interacting subdomains. Although all contribute to diffusion, the proline-rich regions primarily act as persistent anchors, whereas the MT-binding repeats contribute most of the net translational displacement along the lattice. Together, these distinct dynamic roles give rise to a partially coordinated yet asynchronous diffusion mechanism. Electrostatic perturbations primarily altered the dynamics of the directly perturbed domain, supporting a locally regulated mechanism. Both the charge and the flexibility of the CTTs were essential for this mechanism: neutralizing the β-tubulin tails had the strongest effect on Tau binding and mobility, and stiffening the tails weakened PRR anchoring. Moreover, Tau segments transiently wrap around individual CTTs, allowing them to remain attached while rearranging. Together, these findings provide a molecular mechanism for Tau diffusion and illustrate how multivalent intrinsically disordered proteins can reconcile persistent substrate association with efficient one-dimensional exploration.

papers.title: Spin Relaxation Rates of Collagen-Associated Water Using Molecular Dynamics Simulations
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: Collagenous tissues such as articular cartilage and tendon are central to joint function, and their microstructures are routinely probed using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). A key feature influencing MRI contrast in these tissues is the spin relaxation behavior of water in the vicinity of collagen, which is also closely linked to the origin of the magic-angle effect. In this study, we use molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the nuclear magnetic resonance spin relaxation rate constants 1/T1 and 1/T2 of water protons near a collagen peptide at room temperature by evaluating the zero-frequency spectral density J(0). A model system consisting of water surrounding a single isolated tropocollagen fragment was employed. To balance the computational cost and statistical accuracy, trajectory data were systematically truncated following a series of tests assessing the relative influence of trajectory length and ensemble size on relaxation estimates for bulk water. The results indicate that the presence of collagen predominantly affects water molecules within the first hydration shell, while outer shells exhibit behavior approaching that of bulk water. Accurate estimation of relaxation rates using standard Redfield theory was found to be challenging because of significant variability in the residence times of water molecules within individual hydration shells, leading to uneven trajectory lengths. To mitigate artifacts arising from this variability, ensemble-averaged spectral density functions were fitted to Lorentzian forms, resulting in an improved stability and accuracy of the computed relaxation rates. Analysis of hydration-shell-resolved dynamics reveals a monotonic decrease in relaxation rates from the first to the third hydration shell, highlighting the strong influence of the protein proximity on water dynamics. These findings demonstrate the sensitivity of spin relaxation to the local hydration structure and provide a computational framework for systematically probing relaxation properties of collagen-associated water in different hydration shells. The approach offers a pathway toward more realistic modeling of fibrillar collagen networks under varying environmental conditions with implications for interpreting MRI contrast in collagen-rich tissues.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Favorability Zones for the Selective Recovery of Critical Elements
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: Increased use of modern technologies has triggered a need to secure the supply chain of critical minerals. This can be potentially achieved through their separation and recovery from waste and industrial streams. To begin to address this need, we adapt Lackner’s thermodynamic calculations for carbon capture from air to define thermodynamic favorability zones consistent with mineral concentrations from various waste streams. These calculations are based on the use of an ideal sorbent, allowing for the determination of the minimum energy a sorbent would need to drive the concentration of ions in solution from an initial concentration (C1) to a final equilibrium concentration (C2). Our analysis focuses on dilute solutions in which full dissociation of ionic species can be assumed. We find that when the initial concentration of the ion in solution is sufficiently low (C1 ≤ 1 × 10–6 mol kg–1) solutions approach ideal behavior, and the free energy of sorption becomes independent of ion identity establishing a free energy limit of approximately −13.64 kcal mol–1 for near-quantitative capture. Conversely, in concentrated solutions, nonideal activities manifest differences in the required sorption free energy based on ion size and charge. We observed that as concentration increases, the necessary free energy of sorption becomes less negative, and an inherent selectivity for monovalent over multivalent ions emerges. This selectivity collapses at both the infinitely dilute limit and near-quantitative capture. These results suggest that solution concentration is not just a boundary condition for ion separation processes, but a potentially tunable design parameter that governs both energetic cost and intrinsic electrostatic selectivity.

papers.title: Theoretical Unimolecular Decomposition Kinetics of Dimethyl, Diethyl, and Ethyl Methyl Carbonates and Their Fluorinated Counterparts
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: Dialkyl carbonates are relevant as sustainable fuel components and as lithium-ion battery electrolyte solvents, where their decomposition chemistry is important for combustion behavior, gas generation, and fire safety. In this work, the unimolecular decomposition kinetics of dimethyl carbonate, diethyl carbonate, ethyl methyl carbonate, and their fluorinated counterparts were investigated using the DLPNO–CCSD(T)/CBS // B97M-V/cc-pVTZ level of theory in combination with RRKM/Master Equation simulations. The resulting potential energy surfaces, bond dissociation energies, thermodynamic properties, and temperature- and pressure-dependent rate coefficients provide a consistent database for kinetic modeling of regular and fluorinated dialkyl carbonates. For the nonfluorinated compounds, the decomposition chemistry is governed by low-barrier molecular pathways, with diethyl carbonate (DEC) and ethyl methyl carbonate (EMC) predominantly forming alkoxyformic acids and ethylene, followed by rapid secondary decomposition to alcohols and carbon dioxide. Fluorination was found to generally strengthen C–H bonds and to suppress the dominant alkoxyformic acid-yielding pathways in fluorinated dialkyl carbonates with ethyl moieties. In contrast, fluorination of dimethyl carbonate decreases its stability because an energetically accessible F atom migration pathway accelerates fDMC decomposition by several orders of magnitude. Comparison with available experimental speciation data shows that the present rate coefficients perform comparably to existing models for DMC and DEC, have limited observable impact for EMC under the investigated high-temperature conditions, and improve CO predictions for fDEC pyrolysis. Among the investigated fluorinated carbonates, methyl 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl carbonate (fEMC) emerges as the most promising candidate in terms of combined unimolecular chemical stability and thermal buffering capacity, motivating further experimental and modeling studies of its potential as a safer lithium-ion battery solvent.

papers.title: Construction of Potential Energy Surface for the PH2+ System and Quantum Dynamics Study of the P+ + H2 Reaction
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: A globally accurate potential energy surface for the 13A″ excited state of PH2+ is constructed by fitting extensive ab initio energies obtained from multireference configuration interaction calculations with the aug-cc-pV(Q+d)Z and aug-cc-pV(5+d)Z basis sets. The topographical features of the potential energy surface are examined in detail and are found to be in excellent agreement with previously reported results. Notably, when the reaction proceeds through the T-shaped geometry, intersystem crossing between the 13A″ and 21A′ potential energy surfaces, driven by spin–orbit coupling, gives rise to nonadiabatic reaction channel. Furthermore, dynamical calculations for the 13A″ state were carried out using the time-dependent wave packet method, showing that at a fixed temperature, increasing the initial rotational quantum number significantly raises the thermal rate constant. The newly developed potential energy surface provides a reliable foundation for investigating the reaction dynamics and for constructing larger phosphorus- and hydrogen-containing systems. Further nonadiabatic dynamical calculations are required to quantitatively assess the role of electronic transitions in the reaction mechanism.

papers.title: Chalcogen-Controlled Triplet Harvesting in Benzophenone-Derived Chromophores: A Theoretical Investigation of Excited-State Relaxation Pathways
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: Efficient triplet-state harvesting in organic chromophores is governed by a delicate interplay between excited-state energetics, orbital character, spin–orbit coupling, and vibronic coupling. Here, we present a systematic theoretical investigation of chalcogen substitution in benzophenone-derived chromophores, in which the carbonyl oxygen is progressively replaced by sulfur and selenium. Three molecular families were examined: benzophenone, Michler’s ketone, and 4,4′-dinitrobenzophenone, together with their thio- and seleno-analogues. Density functional theory (DFT) and time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) calculations were used to characterize excited-state energetics, absorption and emission properties, natural transition orbitals (NTOs), spin–orbit coupling (SOC) matrix elements, quantitative hole–electron descriptors, interfragment charge-transfer character (IFCT), and state-specific intersystem-crossing (ISC) rates. Chalcogen substitution systematically stabilizes the low-lying excited states, produces pronounced red shifts in the lowest absorption bands, and reorganizes the singlet–triplet manifold. Simultaneously, the heavier chalcogen atoms markedly enhance SOC. For the strongest retained S1 → T2 SOC channels, the calculated SOC increases from 35.96 to 134.19 and 645.36 cm–1 across BP, TBP, and SBP, respectively, with analogous O → S → Se enhancements in the substituted series. Quantitative NTO, hole–electron, and IFCT analyses show that these SOC trends are coupled to excitation localization, hole–electron overlap, and charge-transfer character. NTO analysis reveals that the lowest singlet excited states are predominantly of (nπ*) character, whereas the higher triplet states relevant to strong SOC frequently possess substantial (ππ*) character, providing favorable El-Sayed-type spin-conversion pathways. The results therefore show that chalcogen identity, orbital-character change, and the spatial distribution of the participating excited states act cooperatively in controlling singlet–triplet coupling in these benzophenone-derived chromophores.

papers.title: Intra- and Intermolecular Interactions in Cellobiose: Benchmarking Accelerated Computational Methods for Cellulose
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
papers.abs: Access to accelerated computational methods at the electronic and atomistic scales is important in materials modeling, as it will allow more realistic system descriptions. Against this background, a systematic study of a range of electronic/atomistic methods applied to cellobiose monomers and dimers is presented, with the aim of identifying methods that achieve a significant acceleration of cellulose computations compared to hybrid DFT methods while retaining adequate accuracy. We benchmark such methods, namely the semiempirical quantum-mechanical tight-binding GFNn-xTB (n = 1,2) and G-xTB methods, the MACE-OMol-0 machine-learning potential, and the CHARMM36 force field, against three DFT references (ωB97M-V, B3LYP-D3, PBE-D3) for gas-phase cellobiose monomers and dimers, focusing on structures, energies, and vibrational properties. Cellobiose monomers and dimers, as presented in this work, do not represent the structural complexity of cellulose, but they provide tractable structural models for assessing the qualities of the selected computational models regarding cellobiose–cellobiose intermolecular interactions that are also present in cellulose. We find that (i) the chain–chain and sheet–sheet dimer interactions are of comparable magnitude, suggesting that both intermolecular dispersion and hydrogen bonding make important contributions to dimer stability, so accurate treatment of noncovalent interactions the calculations is essential; (ii) GFN2-xTB and G-xTB reproduce most conformations well, with a speed-up of two to three orders-of magnitude compared to the DFT calculations, but fail for puckered, strained conformations, artificially improving apparent dimer-energy agreement with DFT; (iii) MACE reaches near-DFT accuracy with a further order of magnitude speed-up, although in a few cases fails to reproduce the hybrid DFT conformations. This is especially true for the chain–chain dimer structure, which is also reflected in a significant deviation of the chain–chain energy-distance potential curve, which highlights the importance of system-dependent model validation (as was done here) and suggests a need for model fine-tuning for cellulose systems; (iv) CHARMM36 has some conformational and energetic limitations,but being 30,000× faster than G-xTB (itself orders of magnitude faster than DFT), remains practical for qualitative studies.

papers.title: Rigid Molecule Packing Similarity Index Based on Dual Quaternions
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
papers.abs: Mapping comparisons between periodic 3D rigid-molecule (or fixed molecular conformer) arrangements to a scalar value, typically referred to as a similarity index, is essential in fields such as crystal structure prediction (CSP) and molecular engineering. Evaluating crystal lattice similarity is crucial for filtering random structure pools and differentiating polymorphs. Here, we introduce a configurational similarity index based on dual quaternions to simultaneously capture relative rigid-molecule (fixed molecular-conformer) positions and orientations in crystal lattices. Within this framework, pairs of molecular configurations with known atomic correspondence are compared using a metric derived from the product of their dual quaternions. After validating the metric on water dimer configurations, we employ it to contrast clusters of molecules representing different molecular packing motifs. This pairwise comparison is condensed into a single index, Drt, which measures total crystal packing similarity. Using Drt to screen pools of randomly generated structures for oxalic acid, maleic hydrazide, and formamide, we successfully retrieve packing motifs similar to the experimental references. Upon geometry optimization, these identified structures converge to the corresponding optimized experimental configurations, highlighting the reliability of this metric for integration into CSP methodologies.

papers.title: Real-Time Multidimensional Spectroscopy for Organic Molecules in Cavities: Dark-State Dynamics and Optical Signatures
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
papers.abs: Ultrafast multidimensional spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful tool for probing organic exciton–polaritons in optical microcavities, revealing rich dynamical properties at the femtosecond timescale. However, the dark states and their crosstalk with polaritons still remain challenging, due to the ultrafast dynamics and optical responses that lead to large ambiguities in the interpretation of time-domain spectroscopic experiments, which signify the properties of highly excited states. Here, we develop a fully quantum-mechanical approach to simulate ultrafast two-dimensional polaritonic spectroscopy (2DPS) of organic systems with strong vibronic coupling. By incorporating the time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (TD-DMRG) method into spectroscopic simulations, our approach enables direct visualization of dark-state dynamics and their excited-state absorption (ESA) signals in organic molecules confined in Fabry–Pérot cavities with realistic vibrational environments. Our results reveal two distinct classes of dark states, namely, lower-polariton (LP) polarons and dark polaritons, which are clearly distinguishable from bright polaritons in 2DPS signals. Time-resolved spectra further exhibit their relaxation dynamics, showing by separated timescales and pathways for energy migration, e.g., ∼200 fs for polaron decoupling. Furthermore, these findings provide new theoretical insights into light-induced phases in organic materials and offer guidance for the design of polaritonic devices.

papers.title: Carbyne‐Terminated Carbon‐Flanked Noble‐Gas Cations: Stability and Asymmetric C–Ng–C Bonding (NgHe–Rn)
papers.jname: Journal of Computational Chemistry
papers.abs: Carbyne‐terminated, carbon‐flanked noble‐gas cations CH 2 NgCR + (Ng = He–Rn; R = CH, N, P, As) serve as a minimal platform for carbon‐only coordination of noble gases and for tuning asymmetric C–Ng–C bonding. Geometry optimizations and thermochemistry were performed at the MP2/def2‐TZVPP level. Most systems adopt a C 2v Y‐shaped structure, with CH 2 HeCCH + and CH 2 NeCCH + as C s exceptions. In contrast, no bound minima were located for CH 2 HeCN + and CH 2 NeCN + at the MP2 level, although Y‐shaped structures were obtained at the DFT level. The singlet is the lowest electronic state for most bound systems, although CH 2 NeCCH + and CH 2 ArCP + have lower‐energy triplet states, while CH 2 ArCCH + and CH 2 XeCP + show near‐degenerate spin states. A dissociation network considering different fragmentation limits and the CH 2 spin state was used to assess thermodynamic stability. The bound He and Ne complexes are destabilized by three‐body homolytic fragmentation, whereas dissociation into CH 2 (t) + NgCR + generally provides the most relevant dissociation limit for the heavier analogues. Several Ar and Kr derivatives remain close to thermoneutrality or are slightly unstable at 298 K, while the Xe and Rn systems are thermodynamically protected with respect to the dissociation pathways considered. NPA, Mayer bond‐order, QTAIM, and AdNDP analyses reveal pronounced asymmetry: the H 2 C–Ng contact is weak and becomes closed‐shell for Ne, whereas Ng–CR exhibits shared‐shell character and near‐single‐bond Mayer indices for Ar–Rn. EDA, performed at the ωB97X–D3/def2–TZVPP level, indicates predominantly electrostatic H 2 C–Ng stabilization and a larger orbital contribution to the Ng–CR interaction in the heavier noble‐gas systems.

papers.title: Sc 2 @ C 66 . Spherical Aromaticity in a Markedly Ellipsoidal Endohedral Metallic Fullerene
papers.jname: Journal of Computational Chemistry
papers.abs: Incorporation of metallic atoms into fullerenes leads to the characterization of nonclassical cage landscapes, highlighting the markedly ellipsoidal Sc 2 @C 2v (4059)‐C 66 structure. In this work, we set out to explore Sc 2 @C 2v (4059)‐C 66 and its Stone‐Wales transformation isomer (Sc 2 @ C 2v ‐(3441)‐C 66 ) in terms of the resulting characteristics provided by the donation of six electrons from the metallic atoms into the π‐electron C 66 kernel in terms of induced magnetic field characteristics. The Sc 2 @C 66 species shows a long/short axis ratio surpassing that of C 70 , featuring two sets of three consecutively fused pentagons at the poles. From the resulting electron transfer from two encapsulated Sc atoms to the C 66 cage, resulting in a 72 π‐electron system that fulfills Hirsch's 2( N + 1) 2 spherical aromaticity rule ( N = 5). Our results support the formation of a spherical aromatic endohedral metallic fullerene (EMF) despite the elongated shape, which shows the absence of a direct Sc‐Sc bond. The Stone‐Wales transformation connecting both isomers modulates their local electronic and magnetic properties, having a lesser impact on the global aromatic properties. These findings highlight the persistence of spherical aromatic characteristics and adaptability in relation to structural rearrangements within an ellipsoidal EMF, as a suitable building block for applications in supramolecular chemistry and related fields.

papers.title: Ab initio -based intermolecular potential for normal hydrogen, orthohydrogen, and parahydrogen: Prediction of thermodynamic behavior
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: An ab initio-based intermolecular potential is reported for normal hydrogen, orthohydrogen, and parahydrogen. Molecular simulations for thermodynamic properties and calculations of the second virial coefficients demonstrate very good agreement with reference values for both the nuclear spin isomers of hydrogen. The thermodynamic behavior studied includes vapor–liquid equilibria, energy, enthalpy, heat capacities, isochoric pressure coefficient, isobaric thermal expansion coefficient, isothermal compressibility, Joule–Thomson coefficient, and speed of sound. The simulations extend from low (cryogenic) to ambient temperatures and pressures of up to 100 MPa. Quantum effects have an important influence on the behavior of these properties, which, in some cases, are not limited to the intermolecular potential contribution to the energy. That is, the enthalpy, heat capacities, Joule–Thomson coefficient, and speed of sound are also significantly affected by quantum effects on the kinetic energy. The simulation values may be more reliable than existing reference data in some instances. This is particularly the case for the thermodynamic properties of orthohydrogen that cannot be measured directly.
papers.zh: 基于从头算方法的正氢、邻氢和对氢的分子间势：热力学行为的预测

papers.title: Automatic generation of exchange–correlation response kernels
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: Computing density-functional response properties requires contracting derivatives of the exchange–correlation (xc) energy with perturbed densities on a grid. While the xc functional’s derivatives have long been available to high orders from libraries such as Libxc, the surrounding contraction layer—the chain rule that combines them with the grid-based basis-function and density data into the total xc contribution—has instead been hand-derived and hand-coded in every program, for every functional family, spin case, and property. We present libxckernel, a library that automatically generates this layer by symbolic differentiation. The xc functional’s ingredients are expressed as sesquilinear forms in the density matrix, so the xc energy can be differentiated to any order while the functional derivatives remain opaque. The basis functions and the orbital coefficients may both be complex. The chain rule then produces any xc matrix element: Fock matrices, orbital Hessians, or any other response terms of any order. Terms sharing a pattern are collapsed for efficiency. Extensible plugins emit the expressions as NumPy Einstein sums, compiled C++ kernels with C/Fortran interfaces, or host-program specific source code. libxckernel is free and open-source software under the BSD-3-Clause license, enabling rapid implementation of functionality missing from many electronic structure programs. We demonstrate it by extending Psi4 with meta-generalized gradient approximation (mGGA) response kernels for orbital stability analysis and time-dependent density-functional theory (TD-DFT), GGA and mGGA analytic nuclear Hessians, and exact quadrature grid response, as well as by extending GPAW with mGGA and triplet TD-DFT kernels and gradient-corrected kernels for periodic dielectric response.

papers.title: Global coarse-grained simulation of hierarchical self-assembly in ABn dendron-like giant molecules: Phase behavior, molecular packing, and the role of rigidity
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: We present a global dissipative particle dynamics simulation study of hierarchical self-assembly in ABn dendron-like giant molecules, drawing upon the experimental platform where hydrophilic and hydrophobic polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane cages serve as the amphiphilic building blocks. Without imposing any pre-assumed structural bias, our coarse-grained model spontaneously evolves from disordered melts into lamellar, double gyroid, hexagonal cylinder, and spherical micelle phases as the number of hydrophobic peripheral units increases—a sequence that faithfully mirrors experimental observations. A key innovation lies in comparing three topologically isomeric representations of the molecular building block: a rigid cage, a flexible chain, and a ring. This systematic comparison reveals that molecular rigidity alone can significantly alter phase boundaries and reduce micelle sizes, a finding that disentangles the role of shape persistence from that of composition or molecular weight. Our simulations further uncover hidden organizational features, including ordered linker arrays within lamellar interphases and the emergence of perforated lamellar structures upon linker elongation. While complete ordering into Frank–Kasper lattices remains computationally demanding, statistical characterizations of the spherical micelles consistently recover experimental trends, affirming the predictive capacity of our approach. This work establishes global coarse-grained simulation as an effective tool for exploring the rich phase behavior of giant molecules and lays the groundwork for the modular, in silico design of programmable supramolecular materials.

papers.title: Quantum critical behavior in chains of hindered dipolar planar rotors
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: We study the ground-state properties of linear chains of dipolar planar rotors hindered by a sixfold on-site potential, a model motivated by water molecules confined in the hexagonal cavities of beryl. Using density matrix renormalization group calculations, we locate the quantum phase transition between the disordered and ferroelectrically ordered phases using the von Neumann entanglement entropy and the Binder ratio of the polarization. A sweep of the sixfold pinning strength shows that increasing hindrance shifts the critical dipolar coupling gc to smaller values. These results suggest that crystal-field hindrance can promote, rather than suppress, dipolar ordering. This work has implications for ferroelectricity and quantum-device tuning in confined molecular rotors.

papers.title: Highly excited 3Πg electronic states of the cesium dimer— Ab initio predictions and experimental observation of the 63Πg state
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: We report the results of an experimental investigation of the highly excited 6Πg3 electronic state of the Cs2 molecule. In addition, we present ab initio potential energy curves for all Cs2Πg3 electronic states up to the 6s+7d limit, calculated using the pseudopotential method. Rovibrational levels of the excited triplet state were observed experimentally using the perturbation facilitated optical–optical double resonance technique, with levels of the AΣu+1∼bΠu3 mixed manifold serving as intermediate states. A progression of P and R branch probe laser resonances was detected by measuring laser-induced fluorescence to the aΣu+3 state as a function of the probe laser frequency. For select rovibrational levels of the 6Πg3 state, dispersed fluorescence to the aΣu+3 state and the AΣu+1∼bΠu3 manifold was recorded and compared with Franck–Condon factor calculations to determine the state multiplicity and vibrational numbering. Using the electric dipole selection rules and comparison with our ab initio results allowed the experimentally observed levels to be assigned to the 6Πg3 state. Term values of the 270 observed rovibrational levels of the 6Πg3 state were fit to a Dunham expansion. From the fitted Dunham constants, a potential energy curve was constructed using the Rydberg–Klein–Rees method.
papers.zh: 铯二聚体的高激发3Πg电子态——63Πg态的从头计算预测和实验观测

papers.title: Fractional viscoelasticity in transient unentangled polymer networks
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: Stress relaxation in transient polymer networks often shows extended power-law behavior, G(t) ∼ t−β, where the exponent β frequently departs from the value 1/2 predicted by the sticky Rouse model and its variants. We introduce the fractional inhomogeneous Rouse model (FIRM), which uses a generalized Langevin equation driven by fractional Gaussian noise of exponent α, while retaining heterogeneous bead friction to represent sticky cross-links. Thus, FIRM unifies subdiffusive sticker dynamics and chain heterogeneity within a single framework. We show that the relaxation modulus G(t) can be represented as a linear combination of the squares of Mittag–Leffler functions. For homogeneous chains, it recovers two power-law regimes, t−α/2 and t−2α, on either side of the Rouse relaxation time. Fitting FIRM to stress relaxation data for an imine-based polystyrene vitrimer shows that α < 1 captures the shape of G(t) over finite observation windows. FIRM accommodates both Arrhenius and non-Arrhenius temperature dependences in the effective activation energy. We derive expressions for dynamic properties, such as mean-squared displacement and dielectric response, and outline how generalized memory kernels extend the framework to real materials. Together, these results suggest novel ways in which data from rheology, dielectric spectroscopy, scattering, and other experimental methods may be incorporated into a molecular model.
papers.zh: 瞬态非缠结聚合物网络中的分数粘弹性

papers.title: Effect of added salts on the interfacial dynamics of monovalent metal ions and model water-soluble polymers
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: Traditional theories of electrolyte and polyelectrolyte solutions overlook ion and polymer hydration, yielding an overly idealized perspective of the thermodynamic and dynamic properties of these solutions. In particular, the propensity of certain ions to increase or decrease the water diffusion coefficient at low solution concentrations is poorly understood, a phenomenon that correlates strongly with the Hofmeister series, which describes the influence of salts on the solubility and self-assembly of synthetic and biological macromolecules, as well as colloidal particles. These ion-specific effects have profound ramifications in diverse biological, medical science, and technological applications. We address the general problem of understanding ion and uncharged water-soluble polymer hydration through molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of representative water-soluble polymers, polyacrylamide and polyethylene oxide, in aqueous salt solutions. Careful attention is given to the capacity of our model to reproduce observed trends of added monovalent salts on the diffusion coefficient of water. Reproducing these ion-specific trends in the mobility of water has been a recurrent challenge in prior MD simulations of aqueous solutions based on a physically realistic model of water. Our work on salt solutions represents an important advance on which we build our modeling of aqueous polymer solutions with added salts. Simulations of our model polymers reveal an extended nanoscale dynamic hydration layer having a scale on the order of 1 nm, in which the mobility is perturbed from its bulk value, and the mobility gradient in this layer appears to obey a near universal functional form.

papers.title: An efficient approach to estimate electronic couplings in molecular pairs using molecular orbital grids: A generalization of CubeMap
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: Estimating electronic couplings (V) is essential to understanding the fundamental electron-transfer process between molecular systems and, consequently, developing computationally efficient approaches for their fast, yet accurate estimation is central to (bio)chemistry and materials science. We have recently proposed a novel and ultrafast approximation, called CubeMap [R. Rubert-Albiol et al., J. Chem. Phys. 162, 064105 (2025)], to evaluate V in molecular pairs. CubeMap exploits the well-known linear relationship (V = C · S) between V and the molecular orbital overlap integral (S) via a fitting constant C. Nevertheless, the original CubeMap formulation required an initial system-specific parameterization, limiting the broad and general applicability of the method for the final users. In this work, we present a significant generalization of the CubeMap method by setting a global scaling factor using a wide and diverse library (more than 80 π-conjugated molecules and 42 000 dimers). The new protocol removes the initial molecule-specific fitting, which was a computational burden, and broadens its scope for non-specialized users in a “black-box” manner. The CubeMap approach has also been extended to deal with semi-flexible molecules with minimal user input, mitigating errors arising from peripheral and/or floppy substituents. Validation across the database shows a good agreement with reference electronic structure calculations, maintaining reasonable mean absolute errors, yet with an important speed-up of up to three orders of magnitude and agreement on the resulting statistical distributions. CubeMap therefore constitutes a reliable tool for numerous evaluations of electronic couplings between molecular units and is, therefore, of great interest for large-scale simulations of charge transport.

papers.title: Interaction embedding via factorized linear models for multi-element machine learning interatomic potentials
papers.jname: The Journal of Chemical Physics
papers.abs: Linear machine-learning interatomic potentials, such as the Ultra-Fast Force Field (UF3), deliver near-density functional theory accuracy at low computational cost. Their number of parameters, however, grows combinatorially with the number of chemical species, limiting their use on multi-element systems. We address this scaling problem with pseudo-interaction UF3 (PI-UF3), a factorized linear model in which the Z(k) real k-body potentials are expressed as linear combinations of a small number P(k) ≪ Z(k) of shared pseudo-interactions. Learned element embeddings are standard in nonlinear potentials; inside a linear model, the embedding becomes a rank constraint on the coefficient matrix of each body order, and the resulting bilinear problem is trained with alternating least squares, where each block update is one closed-form linear solve. We benchmark PI-UF3 on a five-element refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) and a subset of MD22, training on forces, with restarts and cross-validation. On the chemically homogeneous HEA, compression acts as implicit regularization: with three-body terms included, PI-UF3’s test force root-mean-squared error drops below the unfactorized UF3 baseline with 3% of the baseline’s parameters on the predefined split and 7% on every cross-validation fold, and the maximally compressed model recovers a chemically meaningful ordering of homonuclear interaction strengths consistent with experimental bulk melting temperatures. On the chemically heterogeneous MD22 subset, where UF3 is not expressive enough to overfit, PI-UF3 approaches the baseline from above and reaches parity with it at about two thirds of the parameter count. Compression thus regularizes only where the unfactorized model overfits, while a parameter reduction is available in both regimes.

papers.title: Phase-Dependent Photoinduced Lattice Deformation in Lead Halide Perovskites
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Lead halide perovskites (LHPs) display rich carrier–lattice coupling phenomena─including photostriction and large-polaron formation─that underpin their unique optoelectronic properties. However, experimentally observed photoinduced structural responses vary considerably across studies, and the microscopic mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we employ occupation-constrained density functional theory to investigate photoinduced structural distortions in CsPbBr3 and MAPbBr3. We find that the structural deformations are significant in the tetragonal phase but negligible in the orthorhombic and cubic phases. This phase selectivity arises from symmetry-induced level splitting at the band edges. These findings highlight the critical role of structural phase in governing photostriction and carrier–lattice responses in LHPs.

papers.title: Ad-Lib: An Adsorption-Energy Descriptor Library for Physically Interpretable Catalyst Informatics
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: A central challenge in heterogeneous catalyst informatics is developing descriptors that capture catalyst behavior while remaining physically interpretable. Catalyst–reaction-species interactions provide a basis for representing heterogeneous catalytic reactions. Here, a high-throughput density functional theory adsorption-energy library (Ad-Lib) is constructed, and designed descriptors are applied to oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) and CO2 methanation, with OCM as the principal case study. Mapping catalysts in an adsorption-energy-defined interaction space provides a landscape of catalytic performance. The utility of this representation for describing catalytic behavior is further demonstrated through machine learning and SHAP analysis. This work establishes the multidimensional adsorption-energy space as a reaction-informed, physically grounded framework for heterogeneous catalyst informatics.

papers.title: Chirality in Resonance Energy Transfer: Donor-Imprinted Ellipticity in Achiral Acceptor Emission
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Chirality pervades chemistry, yet the Förster mechanism of resonance energy transfer (RET), widely applied in biostructure analysis, is blind to molecular handedness. Through a quantum-electrodynamical analysis that restores the magnetic-dipole contributions neglected in the Förster picture, we identify two ways in which a chiral donor imprints its handedness on energy transfer. The transfer rate becomes handedness-dependent but only in a genuinely chiral environment. Additionally, a chiral donor imprints a circularly polarized signature onto the fluorescence of an otherwise achiral acceptor, a signal that survives in isotropic solution and reverses for the opposite enantiomer of the donor. Compact orientation maps convert these effects into design rules linking geometry to handedness-dependent output, peaking in complementary arrangements. The results may help explain recent chirality-transfer experiments and pave the way for circularly polarized light sources and chirality sensors in which brightness and handedness originate in different molecules.

papers.title: Correlation between Crystal-Structure Evolution and Valence-Band Characteristics among Multiple 1T-TaS2 Phases
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: 1T-TaS2 is a two-dimensional strongly correlated electron material featuring broadband saturable absorption. Although the band structures of 1T-TaS2 in distinct phases have been reported, the correlation between the evolution of electronic band structure and crystal structure across different phases remains rarely explored. In this work, the two-component exothermic signature in heating differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements points to sequential overlapping charge-density-wave (CDW) rearrangements for the commensurate phase (Cp) to intermediate phase (Ip) to triclinic phase (Tp) evolution, rather than a single sharp transition. Additionally, temperature-dependent synchrotron-based angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), combined with variable-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectroscopy, and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations, is employed to unravel the interplay between valence-band electronic structures and crystal structures of 1T-TaS2 in its commensurate, intermediate, and triclinic phases. This work provides valuable references for the practical utilization of 1T-TaS2 under varied thermal conditions.

papers.title: Molecular Factors Governing Triboelectric Energy Conversion: From Surface Chemistry to Dynamic Charge Transport
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Triboelectric energy conversion has emerged as a promising platform for self-powered electronics, yet its underlying contact electrification mechanisms remain actively debated. In this Perspective, we present a unified framework connecting interfacial chemistry, dielectric physics, transport kinetics, and surface morphology. Taking the contact potential difference (CPD) as a thermodynamic baseline, we examine how chemical functionalization, stoichiometric Fermi-level tuning, and bulk dielectric polarization modulate the driving force for charge transfer. We further highlight how contact–separation or sliding motion promotes carrier transport by overcoming potential barriers through dynamic mechanisms such as energy dissipation, phonon excitation, thermoelectric effect, and flexoelectric coupling. Finally, we discuss how multiscale morphological engineering amplifies effective contact area and strain gradients to reinforce charge exchange. By unifying these fundamental modalities, this Perspective provides rational design principles for next-generation triboelectric materials and high-performance nanogenerators.

papers.title: Adiabatic Populations for High-Dimensional Quantum Simulations Using Matrix Product State Sampling
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Electronic state populations are central quantities in nonadiabatic dynamics, with different electronic representations conveying different information. The populations of diabatic states, which preserve electronic character, offer chemically intuitive interpretations of dynamical simulations. The populations of adiabatic states, which are simply the energy-ordered eigenstates of the electronic Hamiltonian, track the electronic relaxation of the system. For high-dimensional quantum simulations, adiabatic populations have remained essentially inaccessible due to the high intrinsic rank of the diabatic-to-adiabatic transformation. Here, we present a method that bypasses this problem, using Ferris and Vidal’s Monte Carlo sampling approach to estimate adiabatic populations from matrix product state (MPS) wave functions. The estimator is unbiased with rigorously bounded statistical error, has computational scaling comparable to propagation, and places no additional restriction on the Hamiltonian. We demonstrate converged adiabatic populations for the 24-mode pyrazine and 78-mode BMA radical cation models, whose contrasting dynamics illustrate the necessity of both electronic representations for interpretation. The sampled configurations further enable trajectory-like analyses of wavepacket dynamics and promise to provide rigorous high-dimensional benchmarks for mixed quantum-classical methods.

papers.title: Beyond Droplets: Single-Molecule FRET Illuminates LLPS Dynamics
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) organizes biomolecules into dynamic, membraneless condensates seen in stress granules, nucleoli, and P-bodies, thereby facilitating rapid and reversible cellular compartmentalization related to transcription, RNA processing, and signaling. While LLPS is important for normal physiology, there is mounting evidence that involuntary transitions to solid-like states are involved in neurodegenerative disorders, cancer, and viral pathogenesis. It is difficult to understand the molecular events that regulate LLPS because ensemble techniques blur the inherent heterogeneity and transient interactions. Single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (sm-FRET) fills this gap by providing nanometer-scale resolution of conformational dynamics and intermolecular interactions. Recent sm-FRET studies reveal that IDPs and RNA undergo pronounced conformational redistribution during LLPS, including compaction, expansion, and kinetic slowing that correlate with nucleation, maturation, and pathological transitions. Importantly, these conformational changes are inseparable from the reorganization and exchange of water molecules, which govern solvation free energy, osmotic balance, and interfacial transport across condensate boundaries therefore acting as both a thermodynamic driver and a kinetic regulator of condensate assembly and aging. Here, we review recent applications of sm-FRET to LLPS-associated systems, including tau–RNA cophase separation and SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein assemblies, to illustrate how nanoscale conformational dynamics, hydration energetics, and interfacial transport collectively govern condensate behavior. By integrating sm-FRET-derived observables with phenomenological models of water flux and free energy contributions, we propose a unifying framework that connects molecular insights, hydration-mediated interactions, and disease relevant phase transitions. Together, these insights position sm-FRET as a powerful platform for dissecting the physical chemistry of biomolecular condensates and for guiding the rational development of therapeutic strategies targeting pathological LLPS.

papers.title: Strain Control of the Exciton Dynamics in WS2 Monolayers
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides blend attractive semiconducting electronic properties with remarkable light–matter interaction. Their optoelectronic, photonic, and light-harvesting functionalities are determined by the nonequilibrium behavior of photogenerated charges and excitons, whose resonant energy, effective mass, and mobility depend crucially on the strain applied to the lattice. Nevertheless, very few studies have directly assessed the role of strain in controlling the most relevant photophysical processes occurring on the femto- and picosecond time scales. Here, we report the modulation of the exciton recombination in monolayer WS2 via the application of uniaxial tensile strain. For 1% applied strain the dominant (few-ps) recombination time decreases over the unstrained case by a factor of 2. We ascribe these fast dynamics to the exciton migration toward ultrafast recombination centers and the strain-induced enhancement of this process to an increased exciton diffusion. This trend is confirmed by a corresponding decrease in the calculated electron and hole effective masses for a strained lattice. Such control over the exciton lifetime suggests that strain can play a crucial role in enhancing luminescent and lasing applications as well as for encoding information in excitons.

papers.title: Competing Structural Phases in Lead-Free Zero-Dimensional Guanidinium Bismuth Iodide Perovskite
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Lead-free halogenobismuthates(III) have been attracting attention as nontoxic, stable alternatives to lead halide perovskites, yet their temperature-driven phase behavior is often poorly understood. Here, we present a comprehensive study of the zero-dimensional perovskite-like semiconductor [C(NH2)3]3Bi2I9 (GA3Bi2I9), combining single-crystal X-ray diffraction with calorimetric, dielectric, and light absorption measurements. Five temperature-induced phases have been identified: the high-temperature hexagonal phase I (P63/mmc), the room-temperature orthorhombic phase II (Cmcm), and three low-temperature monoclinic phases III, IV, and V (all of the space group P1121/m) that coexist over an unusually broad temperature range. Throughout, the crystal retains its layered framework of Bi2I93– bioctahedra and guanidinium cations linked by N–H···I hydrogen bonds, while the transitions are driven by cation ordering, reorientations, and displacements, and the concomitant switching of the hydrogen-bonding scheme. Particularly at low temperatures, the subtle modifications in hydrogen bonding and rearrangements of the ions lead to the coexistence and competition of phases whose thermodynamic stability is comparable. Phase transitions in GA3Bi2I9 are highly sensitive to thermal history and internal stress, underscoring the subtlety of structural modifications. The crystal shows negative linear thermal expansion in most phases, distinct dielectric anomalies at the transitions, and a linear narrowing of the optical gap with increasing temperature from 2.36 eV at 80 K to 2.11 eV at 460 K, changing the crystal color from pale orange to almost black.

papers.title: Oxygen Segregation Energetics and Tensile Plasticity of Aluminum Grain Boundaries
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Grain boundary (GB) oxidation plays an important role in determining the chemical and mechanical properties of metals, while its associated structural evolution and deformation mechanisms at the atomic scale are still not fully understood. In this work, we employ reactive molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the tensile behavior of four aluminum tilt-symmetric oxygen-loaded bigrain GBs containing structure units (SUs) “C/D” and “E”. We find that there is a critical oxygen density that controls changes in oxygen-loaded GB structure, as well as the tensile behavior and deformation mechanisms. Below such a critical density, GB tensile yield stress increases because the presence of oxygen hinders dislocation nucleation from SU “E”, but decreases because oxygen favors the phase transformation of GBs with SU “C/D”. Above such a critical density, a dense oxide layer is formed and the dislocation nucleates from the GB oxide layer–grain interface. Whether the dislocation is easy or hard to nucleate is dependent on the mismatch between the amorphous GB oxide layer and the grain because the mismatch is determined by the geometrical orientation of the grain adjacent to the amorphous GB oxide layer. Particularly, the hardening phenomenon seen in the unoxidized GB with SUs “E” may vanish as the GB oxidation deepens because oxygen changes the behavior of dislocation nucleation from SUs “E”. The findings of this study may shed light on the oxidation-modulated behavior and deformation mechanism of metal GBs.
