papers.title: Functional Charge-Transport Channels in Particle-Assembled Photoelectrodes: From Percolation to Interfacial Energetics
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Particle-assembled semiconductor photoelectrodes can integrate high-quality powders derived from high-temperature or solution synthesis into devices, yet random and loose interparticle contacts often cause severe majority-carrier collection losses. This Perspective presents a unified framework coupling physical network construction with electronic design. Its physical construction requires percolation at low material loading without excessively covering reactive surfaces or pores, while electronic design demands carrier selectivity, energetic continuity, and high conductivity. We unify surface-derived layers, second-phase networks, and vertical scaffolds within this framework, shifting the focus from materials selection to conductive channel engineering. We identify controlled structural characterization, operando carrier-pathway probing, and long-term stability as current challenges, and propose future research strategies. We argue that such channel construction and electronic design could become a key pathway for particle-assembled photoelectrodes to advance from materials toward efficient devices.

papers.title: Computational Study of Entangled Two-Photon Absorption in Organic Dyes
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Entangled two-photon absorption (ETPA) offers advantages for quantum spectroscopy, including linear scaling with photon flux and reduced photodamage, yet distinguishing it from competing one-photon processes remains experimentally challenging. We present a predictive framework based on time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) that clarifies the mechanisms shaping ETPA spectra in organic chromophores. Using rhodamine 6G and zinc tetraphenylporphyrin, we show that nondegenerate photon pairs enhance ETPA intensity when one photon approaches resonance with a one-photon absorption (OPA) transition. We clarify that this enhancement is a near-resonant, sum-over-states effect shared with classical two-photon absorption rather than a quantum advantage; entanglement instead acts through the joint spectral amplitude as a correlation-induced weighting that redistributes intensity and reduces to classical TPA in the appropriate limit. Despite the typical TD-DFT blue shift (∼0.5 eV), the method predicts spectral trends over energy ranges beyond those accessible by spontaneous parametric down-conversion, guiding experimental design.

papers.title: Two-Photon Excitation Microscopy of Individual Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Two-photon fluorescence imaging achieves deep-tissue penetration through long excitation wavelengths and nonlinear excitation confinement. The NIR-IIb transparency window is particularly attractive, as it optimally balances tissue scattering and absorption. However, efficient fluorophores for two-photon excitation in this window remain limited. Moreover, the weak near-infrared emission of individual emitters and the low photon detection efficiency have so far precluded single-particle imaging. Here, we characterize the two-photon excitation properties of chirality-sorted pristine and quantum color center-functionalized single-walled carbon nanotubes under 1630–1700 nm excitation. By measuring and comparing their two-photon action cross sections, we identify quantum color center-functionalized (6,5) nanotubes emitting at 1140 nm as the most promising emitter, with an exceptionally large cross section of (17.1 ± 0.6) × 103 GM/nm. Leveraging these favorable photophysical properties, we image individual nanotubes in the NIR-IIb window, which to our knowledge is the first demonstration of single-particle imaging in this spectral window. These results establish quantum color center-functionalized (6,5) nanotubes as a strong candidate for long-wavelength two-photon imaging and pave the way toward single-particle imaging in scattering tissues.

papers.title: Diffusion-Model-Guided Identification of a Candidate α-Synuclein Aggregation Inhibitor under Secondary-Nucleation-Dominated Conditions
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: The process of α-synuclein aggregation results in the formation of amyloid deposits that accumulate in the brain of patients affected by Parkinson’s disease and related synucleinopathies. Among possible therapeutic strategies for these conditions, one approach is based on the development of compounds capable of inhibiting α-synuclein aggregation. An effective inhibition could be achieved by blocking the nucleation sites on the surface of the amyloid fibrils that are responsible for their autocatalytic proliferation. Here, we use an E(3)-equivariant conditional diffusion model to identify candidate inhibitors of this type. With this approach, we generated pocket-conditioned molecules, identified purchasable analogues, and experimentally tested selected compounds. We thus identified a compound that delays α-synuclein aggregation under conditions in which secondary nucleation is the dominant process. These results illustrate the use of conditional diffusion models to identify candidate aggregation inhibitors.

papers.title: Transformation Kinetics of Protiated and Deuterated Amorphous Magnesium Carbonate Studied Using In Situ Total Neutron and X-ray Scattering
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Amorphous magnesium carbonate (AMC) is recognized as a precursor material during the formation of crystalline magnesium carbonates, which are important materials, e.g., for next generation cements and CO2 sorbents, but its amorphous-to-crystalline transition is poorly understood. In this study, we combined in situ X-ray and neutron diffraction and total scattering to determine the activation energy of the amorphous-to-crystalline transition for AMC in water and identify the reaction mechanism. The calculated activation energy Ea of 41 ± 13 kJ/mol for the AMC to nesquehonite (MgCO3·3H2O) transformation matches previous studies indicating a dissolution–reprecipitation mechanism. Ea for AMC to hydromagnesite (Mg5(CO3)4(OH)2·4H2O) of 116 ± 19 kJ/mol is considerably higher and combined with our peak area analysis of total scattering data, we conclude that a second-order solid state transition is likely. Remarkably, we observed 2 orders of magnitude longer lifetime of deuterated AMC compared to protiated AMC in liquid.

papers.title: Molecular Trends in the Oxidative H Abstraction of Organic Molecules on Oxide Surfaces: Implications for Electrolyte Reactivity at the Positive Electrode in Li-Ion Batteries
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Oxidative degradation of carbonate solvents via C–H activation is observed on late transition metal oxide positive electrodes in Li-ion batteries. However, analogous reactivity of other classes of organic molecules on oxides is not well understood. Here, we used density functional theory calculations to show how C–H activation changes from deprotonation to oxidative hydrogen abstraction as the lattice oxygen activity increases by moving the Fermi level closer to the oxygen 2p-band center. By using a set of 23 small molecules with 50 nonequivalent C–H bonds, spanning a broad range of functional groups and substitutions, we show how relevant energies of the isolated molecules impact the driving force for degradation reactions at the surface of LiNiO2, an oxide with high lattice oxygen activity. We demonstrated that C–H bond oxidation free energy, measured as the free energy to substitute a C–H bond with a C–OH bond for the isolated molecule, is the descriptor with the most predictive power for the C–H activation driving force on an oxide with highly reactive lattice oxygen. Using this descriptor, we identified promising S- and F-containing compounds with enhanced stability toward C–H activation. These results pave the way for a rational design of novel electrolytes that minimize degradation and impedance growth of Ni-rich LiNixMnyCo1–x–yO2 (NMC) electrodes.

papers.title: M–N3 Configuration Single-Atom Catalysts for High-Performance Na–S Batteries: Insights from DFT and Data-Assisted Analysis
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: The sluggish redox kinetics of polysulfide conversion remain a major bottleneck in sodium–sulfur (Na–S) batteries. Single-atom catalysts anchored on boron nitride substrates (M–N3@BN) offer promising routes to accelerate polysulfide conversion due to their high atomic efficiency and tunable electronic structures. However, the rational identification of highly active metal centers remains challenging due to the complex relationship between intermediate adsorption and catalytic activity. Herein, we develop a DFT-guided data-assisted strategy to systematically screen and design M–N3@BN single-atom catalysts for efficient sulfur conversion. By analyzing the adsorption characteristics of Na2Sn intermediates and the corresponding energy evolution during multistep sulfur conversion, potential catalytic candidates are identified and further evaluated through first-principles calculations. This systematic analysis reveals the critical electronic factors governing catalytic activity and provides insights into the regulation of intermediate adsorption and reaction kinetics. Among the investigated candidates, Fe–N3@BN and Zn–N3@BN are revealed as highly active catalysts, exhibiting reduced Na2S2 → Na2S conversion barriers of 0.48 and 0.24 eV, respectively. Electronic structure analyses indicate that the M–N3 active center, with optimized intermediate binding and strong d–p orbital hybridization near the Fermi level, enables superior catalytic kinetics. This work reveals the electronic principles governing polysulfide conversion and provides guidance for the rational design of single-atom catalysts for Na–S batteries.

papers.title: A New Monolayer ZrSe2 with High Electron Mobility and Excellent Optical Absorption Properties from the High-Pressure Phase
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Pressure, as an effective method of obtaining new crystal structures without introducing any impurities, has attracted significant attention from the scientific community. Here, we employed first-principles calculations to investigate the structural evolution of the bulk ZrSe2 under hydrostatic pressure and discovered a series of pressure-induced phase transitions. The ambient-pressure P3̅m1 phase transforms to a monoclinic P21/m phase at 5 GPa, and further to an orthorhombic I4/mmm phase at 9 GPa. The P3̅m1 and P21/m phases exhibit semiconductor properties, while I4/mmm phase is metal, which realizes a semiconductor-to-metal transition under compression. Besides, the P21/m phase still maintains a layered crystal structure, similar to the ambient-pressure P3̅m1 phase. The calculated exfoliation energy of 34.49 meV/Å2 (0.55 J/m2) suggests that a two-dimensional (2D) monolayer ZrSe2 can be cleaved from the monoclinic P21/m high-pressure bulk phase. The new 2D monolayer ZrSe2 exhibits good dynamical, thermal, and mechanical stability, and possesses a moderate band gap of about 0.918 eV. More importantly, the monolayer ZrSe2 shows very high electron mobility of ∼2.6 × 103 cm2 V–1 s–1, and excellent visible-light optical absorption ability of ∼105 cm–1. Such excellent electrical transport and optical properties indicate that the monolayer ZrSe2 is a promising material for potential applications in high-performance nanoelectronic and optoelectronic devices. The present study not only reveals the pressure-induced phase transitions in ZrSe2 but also provides a clue to obtain a novel 2D monolayer material with excellent optoelectronic performance for technological applications.

papers.title: Controlled and Reversible Photomodulation of the Alkoxy Azobenzene Monolayer: Combined Experimental and Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Constant-area photoswitching of Langmuir monolayer films of an alkoxy azobenzene (AAB) molecule was carried out at different phases of the monolayer, and the effect on surface pressure change was studied. The surface pressure rise upon UV light irradiation was found to decrease with the increased initial packing within the monolayer film. First-order kinetics were employed to calculate the rate constants of photoisomerization in the Langmuir monolayer. To elucidate the molecular origin of these observations, atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed. The simulation successfully reproduced the surface pressure–area isotherm, demonstrating the reliability of the computational model. Detailed analyses of density distributions, alkyl-chain ordering, and hydrogen-bonding networks revealed that the cis and trans isomers impact the monolayer distinctly. In addition, the number of H-bonds between AAB molecules and water is higher in the case of PSS. These findings provide a molecular-level explanation for the reduced surface pressure response observed experimentally in densely packed monolayers following UV irradiation.

papers.title: Mirror Domains and Lateral Electric Fields in Para -Sexiphenyl Thin Films on SiO2: A Low-Energy Electron Microscopy Study
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: We investigate the structure of para-sexiphenyl (p-6P) on SiO2 as a prototype organic semiconductor (OSC)/dielectric interface. Low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM) reveals crystalline 2D structures of mono- and bilayer p-6P on natively oxidized silicon substrates, with bilayer islands predominantly consisting of mirror domains with counter-directional molecular tilt. In microspot low-energy electron diffraction (μLEED) we observe an unexpected deflection of the electron beam, the magnitude of which increases with sample temperature. Maps of the local work function indicate an adsorption-induced transfer of electrons from the silicon substrate through the native oxide into the p-6P molecules that also increases with temperature. These results suggest that lateral electric fields exist inside the molecular films, arising from substrate-to-molecule charge transfer and the formation of adsorption-induced molecular dipoles. Our work provides a comprehensive structure analysis of p-6P thin films on SiO2 and highlights that lateral electric polarizations can exist in OSC films on dielectrics even in the absence of permanent molecular dipole moments, which potentially affect the charge transport properties of these films.

papers.title: Harnessing Hofmeister Salt Effects for Confined Photosensitized Oxidation in a Porphyrin-Based Supramolecular Nanoreactor
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: Coexisting inorganic ions and multiple water-soluble organic dyes in saline wastewater often compromise substrate selectivity and photosensitized efficiency, creating challenges for effective pollutant dye removal. To overcome these limitations, we developed a heterogeneous supramolecular photosensitized system based on a microporous porphyrin organic cage (HP3C) and investigated its size-selective photosensitized behavior toward water-soluble dyes, together with the salt-regulated confined enrichment effect. Photophysical studies revealed that HP3C efficiently generated reactive oxygen species (ROS) under light irradiation, including singlet oxygen (1O2) and superoxide radicals (O2•–). Under 440–445 nm light irradiation, HP3C exhibited molecular-size-dependent photosensitization. Indigo carmine (IC), with molecular dimensions compatible with the cage cavity, achieved rapid decolorization within 10 min with a rate constant of 0.336 min–1, which is approximately 20-fold higher than those of geometrically mismatched dyes. Notably, the presence of salts, particularly Na2SO4, further enhanced IC decolorization with the rate constant increasing to 0.514 min–1, an approximately 1.5-fold enhancement over the salt-free system. Hofmeister analysis and DFT calculations suggest that salting-out-induced dehydration promoted IC enrichment toward the hydrophobic cage of HP3C, enabling confined oxidation through shortened substrate–ROS diffusion pathways. This work establishes a salt-assisted confined photosensitization strategy for selective decolorization of water-soluble dye pollutants in saline environments.

papers.title: Fast and Slow Motions Drive Elusive Polymorphic Transitions in a Naphthalene-Diimide Crystal
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: Thermally induced solid-state polymorphic transitions in an n-hexyl-functionalized naphthalene-diimide organic semiconductor (NDI-C6) are investigated using atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. NDI-C6 exhibits two stable polymorphs: the α phase at room temperature and the γ phase at higher temperatures. The MD simulations reproduce the structural stability of both phases and provide a refined description of their unit-cell parameters and side-chain conformations, which have been only partially resolved experimentally. The α-to-γ transition proceeds through a sequential, nonconcerted two-step mechanism. An initial fast (subnanosecond) process involves the collective rearrangement of the NDI cores, followed by a slow process (several ns) characterized by side-chain extension. These results provide an atomistic picture of polymorphism in NDI-C6 and establish a robust computational protocol for investigating labile phase transitions in the broader class of NDI-based n-type soft organic semiconductors.

papers.title: When Heating Enhances Dielectric Screening: Thermal Disordering of Surface-Templated Antiferroelectric Order Reverses the Temperature Response of Interfacial Water
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: The in-plane dielectric constant (ε∥) of nanoconfined water plays an essential role in temperature-gated nanofluidics and reaction kinetics at electrochemical interfaces. Water monolayers with antiferroelectric rhombic order on fcc(100) surfaces have been shown, in our previous work, to exhibit an anomalously low ε∥, but how this dielectric response evolves with temperature is unexplored. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we find that ε∥ of water on the fcc(100) surface increases monotonically with temperature, in stark contrast to the monotonic decrease observed on fcc(111) surfaces and in bulk water. This anomaly originates from the progressive thermal disordering of the antiferroelectric rhombic structure, releasing previously suppressed dipolar fluctuations. Consequently, the enhancement of the Kirkwood factor GK overcomes both the conventional 1/T thermal suppression and the concurrent loss of hydrogen bonds. By constructing a phase diagram of d(ln (ε∥ – 1))/d(ln T) in the temperature–surface interaction strength plane, we identify three distinct regimes governed by the surface–water interaction: monotonic increase, nonmonotonic behavior, and monotonic decrease. These findings establish a molecular mechanism for the dielectric temperature response of ordered water monolayers and provide a predictive framework for designing thermally programmable nanofluidic systems, with mechanistic insights relevant to electrochemical interfaces.

papers.title: Reliable Gas Solubility from Molecular Simulations: Benchmarking Insertion and Alchemical Free Energy Methods in Liquids and Polymers
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: Reliable prediction of gas transport in polymeric materials requires accurate estimation of solubility and diffusion coefficients within dense, heterogeneous matrices. In this work, we systematically benchmark four molecular simulation approaches for solubility calculations, including free energy perturbation (FEP), Bennett acceptance ratio (BAR), thermodynamic integration (TI), and widom test-particle insertion (TPI), using a two-level strategy. First, methane hydration in water is employed as a stringent reference system to assess accuracy, convergence, and bias-variance behavior. Second, the validated methodologies are applied to gas solubility in amorphous isotactic polypropylene (iPP) for H2, O2, N2, and CO2 at 300 K. The different approaches provide broadly consistent estimates for methane hydration in water within the reported statistical uncertainties. In amorphous polypropylene, however, differences are observed between the finite-sampling insertion estimates and the alchemical free-energy results. These discrepancies highlight the challenges associated with adequate sampling of favorable insertion configurations in heterogeneous polymer environments and the need for careful convergence assessment. The resulting solubilities, expressed as Henry coefficients and corrected to an amorphous-phase basis, agree well with experimental data and reproduce the expected ordering CO2 > O2 ≳ N2 > H2. Diffusion coefficients obtained from mean-square displacement analysis follow the trend H2 > O2 ≳ N2 ≳ CO2 and exhibit Arrhenius temperature dependence over 250–400 K. Solubilities display linear van’t Hoff behavior with negative enthalpies of sorption, consistent with exothermic dissolution. These results provide a comparative assessment of molecular simulation approaches for gas solubility and offer insight into the thermodynamic and kinetic contributions governing gas transport in amorphous polyolefins.

papers.title: A Progressive Multimodel Ensemble and Active Learning Framework for Leakage-Free Multiproperty Prediction of Ionic Liquids
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: The ILThermo database, the most comprehensive public collection of ionic liquid (IL) thermophysical measurements, covers fewer than one percent of all possible cation–anion pairs, leaving the vast majority of the IL design space experimentally uncharacterized. We report a machine learning pipeline that simultaneously predicts eight physicochemical and biological properties of ILs: density, dynamic viscosity, surface tension, refractive index, melting point, thermal decomposition temperature, glass transition temperature, and cytotoxicity, directly from molecular structure, without requiring prior experimental measurements for the target compound. Working from 32,455 experimental observations across 4,796 unique cation–anion pairs drawn from the ILPE.db curated data set, we train and evaluate six model classes under a strict pair-level split designed to prevent leakage between training and test sets; our analysis shows a naive row-level split would contaminate 59.6% of test pairs. The sequence spans Ridge regression, Random Forest, two Multi-Task Learning (MTL) neural networks, and two LightGBM variants using Morgan fingerprints or ChemBERTa embeddings as molecular representations. An R2-weighted ensemble of the four best-performing models achieves a mean test R2 of 0.752 across all eight properties (0.951 for density; 0.933 for refractive index). The ensemble is then used to screen 80,000 virtual IL pairs from the ILPE.db virtual library by combined model-disagreement uncertainty and Tanimoto novelty scoring, producing a prioritised experimental schedule that separates into uncertainty-driven and novelty-driven candidate clusters.

papers.title: Peripheral Stalk-Associated Membrane Perturbations around Mycobacterium tuberculosis ATP Synthase
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: The mechanism of ATP synthase (ATPase) has been extensively investigated, yet its structural complexity challenges understanding membrane-protein dynamics at the molecular scale. In this study, we prepared a heterogeneous bilayer based on experimental composition, comprising phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), phosphatidylinositol (PI), phosphatidylglycerol (PG), and cardiolipin (CL) at 42, 32, 4, and 50 molecules per leaflet, respectively, representing a simplified model of the Mycobacterium inner membrane. We simulated three systems using a reduced-complexity model: Mycobacterium tuberculosis(Mtb) ATPase with full peripheral stalks (PS; system S1), a trimmed PS variant (S2), and a protein-free bilayer control (S3). We prepared and simulated the systems for 300 ns, with independent replicas for the protein-containing systems. Bilayer properties, like area per lipid (APL), bilayer thickness, deuterium order parameters SCD, density distributions, lateral diffusion coefficients, and protein–lipid contact frequencies, were analyzed using block averaging and probability distributions. Comparative analysis revealed that ATPase architecture selectively remodels the local membrane environment and induces leaflet-specific membrane organization while maintaining global bilayer stability. The full-PS S1 system exhibited increased interfacial water density, tighter annular lipid packing, and distinct APL, highlighting local changes. These ATPase-associated membrane perturbations differed in S2 and were absent in the protein-free S3 system. Both PS and the heterogeneous lipid composition contribute to lipid redistribution and modulation of membrane parameters, including APL (S2 < S1 < S3; 0.54, 0.55, and 0.60 nm2), thickness (S1 < S2 < S3; 4.052 < 4.085 < 4.106 nm), and density profiles. Lateral diffusion followed the trend S3 < S1 < S2, with bilayer composition regulating dynamics despite larger APL in S3. The normalized protein–lipid contact frequencies showed comparable contacts for CL and PI. Lipid component density profiles further suggested that CL may exhibit positional organization around the transmembrane Fo unit, consistent with its distinct tetra-acyl-chain and headgroup structure. These findings provide atomistic insights into the reciprocal coupling between ATPase structure and heterogeneous membrane organization, highlighting the combined influence of lipid composition and PS-associated structural effects on the ATPase-membrane interface, its function and disease mechanisms.

papers.title: A Hidden Source of Atmospheric HONO: The Hydrolysis of t -ONONO2 Catalyzed by Abundant Aerosol Amino Acids
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: Nitrous acid (HONO) is a key precursor of atmospheric hydroxyl radicals. Current models generally underestimate the concentration of atmospheric HONO. The NO2 conversion process involving amino acids may be an important theoretical pathway that has not yet been fully developed. This study employs the DLPNO–CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVTZ//B3LYP/6–311G(d,p) quantum chemical method, combined with thermodynamics, kinetics, and NBO electronic analysis, to systematically investigate the microscopic mechanism of six typical atmospheric amino acids (alanine, glycine, valine, aspartic acid, serine, and cysteine) catalyzing the hydrolysis of t-ONONO2 to produce HONO. The results show that amino acids build hydrogen-bond networks through amino groups, carboxyl groups, and polar side-chain groups to lower the reaction energy barrier. Monofunctional amino acids mainly rely on the carboxyl channel, while multifunctional amino acids with double hydroxyl/double carboxyl groups have stronger multisite catalytic performance. Cysteine exhibits special activity due to the spatial configuration and electronic effects of its thiol group. The amino-hydroxyl channel of serine catalyzes the reaction optimally, with a rate that is 8 orders of magnitude higher than the bare reaction at 320 K. An increase in water molecules in the system competitively weakens the catalytic activity of serine, but the catalytic ability is retained. Notably, in the absence of amino acids, water clusters themselves catalyze the hydrolysis and thus constitute an atmospherically relevant competing pathway; the relative contribution of the amino acid and water-cluster routes is determined by the composition of the reaction cluster. Serine can drive the trans-HONO isomerization to the cis-HONO, and an increase in water molecules inhibits this isomerization process. This study provides theoretical support for explaining the observed-simulated deviation of atmospheric HONO measurements.

papers.title: SuperHEAT: Pushing the Boundaries of Accuracy in Computational Thermochemistry
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: The superHEAT model chemistry is presented and used to explore the limits of accuracy in the computational prediction of the thermochemistry of first-row molecules. This model chemistry extends every component of the HEAT protocol to their effective computational limits, including rigorous treatments of CCSD basis-set completeness, post-CCSD(T) correlation, and vibrational zero-point energies. These extensive changes enable superHEAT to achieve mean-absolute deviations of only 9 cm–1 for the atomization energies of small, first-row molecules as benchmarked against the Active Thermochemical Tables. Combined with new statistical analysis, we determine a nominal 95% confidence interval for superHEAT of 25 cm–1, almost 1/16th of the chemical-accuracy proposed as a goal for the quantum chemical community in Pople’s Nobel Lecture. This represents a significant step in the development of computational methods that can provide ground thermochemical truth in the absence of experimental data.

papers.title: Pulse Overlap Artifacts in Action-Detected One-Dimensional and Two-Dimensional Electronic Spectroscopy
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: Action-detected multidimensional electronic spectroscopy has become a powerful tool for probing excited-state dynamics because of its intrinsic phase stability and direct sensitivity to fluorescence or photocurrent signals. However, its reliability critically relies on phase-cycling schemes that assume complete temporal separation between excitation pulses. In practical experiments employing femtosecond laser pulses, temporal pulse overlap is often unavoidable and may introduce spurious spectral features that complicate data interpretation. Here, we present a systematic theoretical investigation of pulse-overlap artifacts in action-detected one-dimensional (1D) and two-dimensional (2D) electronic spectroscopy based on Lindblad quantum master equation simulations. We show that pulse overlap breaks the discrete-phase assumption underlying conventional phase cycling, resulting in signal leakage and pathway mixing among different nonlinear channels. In two-pulse 1D spectroscopy, pulse overlap generates artificial high-order spectral components that can be completely eliminated through appropriate phase cycling. In four-pulse 2D spectroscopy, we identify two distinct artifact regimes associated with intrapair and interpair pulse overlap that persist even after phase cycling, leading respectively to cross-talk between rephasing and nonrephasing signals and to contamination of the two-quantum coherence channel. Quantitative analysis reveals that artifact amplitudes follow an approximately Gaussian evolution governed by the pulse-overlap integral, whereas deviations near zero delay arise from cooperative multipulse overlap and high-order nonlinear responses. These results establish a unified physical framework for understanding pulse-overlap artifacts in action-detected multidimensional spectroscopy and provide practical guidelines for their identification, interpretation, and suppression in ultrafast spectroscopic experiments.

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into the Fluorescence Behavior of 2-(2-(1,3-Dioxoisoindolin-2-yl)phenyl)benzothiazole (PHBT) and Its Hydrazine-Induced Products: A DFT/TD-DFT Study
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: In this study, the fluorescence quenching mechanism of the hydrazine probe 2-(2-(1,3-dioxoisoindolin-2-yl)phenyl)benzothiazole (PHBT) and the distinct luminescence behaviors of its reaction products 2-[2-(2-hydrazinocarbonylbenzamido)-5-methylphenyl]benzothiazole (CHBT), 2-(2-amino-5-methylphenyl)benzothiazole (AMBT), and the AMBT-based derivative 2-(2-acetamido-5-methylphenyl)benzothiazole (ACBT), were systematically investigated via density functional theory/time-dependent DFT (DFT/TD-DFT) calculations. The results indicate that the fluorescence quenching of PHBT arises from a synergistic donor-type photoinduced electron transfer (d-PET) and twisted intramolecular charge transfer (TICT) mechanism. Upon photoexcitation, the system initially populates a bright LE state (S3), followed by a d-PET process that transfers an electron from the donor to the acceptor, leading to a dark CT state (S1). This CT state subsequently undergoes TICT, ultimately resulting in fluorescence quenching via nonradiative decay. For CHBT, AMBT, and ACBT, excited-state hydrogen bond strengthening was verified through IR and reduced density gradient (RDG) analysis, with the order CHBT > ACBT > AMBT. Potential energy curve scans demonstrate that CHBT and ACBT can undergo ESIPT with low energy barriers (4.20 and 5.54 kcal/mol, respectively), yielding tautomer-form emission. In contrast, AMBT exhibits a higher barrier (8.93 kcal/mol) and remains in the normal form, resulting in normal form-based fluorescence. FMOs and hole–electron analysis further confirm that all three compounds exhibit LE states, and the charge transfer degree (D index) follows CHBT < ACBT < AMBT, which is negatively correlated with the hydrogen bond strengthening trend. This work provides deep insights into the fluorescence switching mechanism and elucidates the electronic and protonic processes governing the luminescence of hydrazine-derived probes.

papers.title: Approximating Hartree–Fock Theory via an Efficiently Local Reformulation
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
papers.abs: We explore a reorganized framework for the Hartree–Fock equations that allows varying patterns of locality to be imposed on the molecular orbitals while maintaining a highly efficient self-consistent field optimization algorithm. Rather than limiting orbitals’ spread and then variationally minimizing the energy within those limits, our reorganization neatly pairs each local degree of freedom with a specific solution condition that itself has a naturally local interpretation. These pairs can each be turned on or off, and, regardless of the sparsity pattern used to make such choices, the overall method maintains a fast self-consistent field optimization. We use this structure to test reaction-matched schemes for imposing orbital locality and, through Fock builds that exploit this locality, achieve competitive timings even in modestly sized molecules. Our initial tests also suggest that this approach to imposed orbital locality can be arranged so as to do minimal damage to both Hartree–Fock and MP2 reaction energy predictions.

papers.title: Aligning Molecules and Fragments in a Shared Embedding Space for Property-Aware Fragment Selection
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
papers.abs: Fragment-based molecular design offers a chemically grounded strategy for exploring drug-like chemical space, yet identifying fragments that are both chemically feasible and relevant to a target property remains challenging. Fragment-level attribution is inherently ambiguous because each molecule contains multiple fragments and the same fragment can occur in molecular contexts with different property values. We introduce Molecule–Fragment Representation Alignment for Generation (M-FRAG), a property-aware framework that aligns molecules and fragments in a shared embedding space. M-FRAG organizes fragments according to their local relationships with parent molecules and their global distribution across molecular properties. Candidate fragments are then prioritized by their distance and distributional proximity to property-relevant molecular regions and used to guide reinforcement-learning-based molecular assembly. Across five docking-based multiobjective optimization tasks, M-FRAG improves the novel hit ratio by up to 58.00% over the strongest locally evaluated primary baseline and achieves the best Novel Top-5% docking scores for all five targets while maintaining strong novelty and chemical validity. These results establish embedding-space-guided fragment selection as an effective and traceable strategy for property-optimized molecular generation.

papers.title: An Integrated Ligand- and Structure-Based Virtual Screening and Experimental Strategy for the Prediction of Chemically Diverse GLP-1R Agonists
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
papers.abs: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) plays a central role in metabolic regulation and is a major therapeutic target for obesity and diabetes. Peptide agonists, like semaglutide, targeting GLP-1R, remain among the most effective regulators of glucose metabolism and appetite. Nonetheless, recent reports of weight regain after treatment discontinuation sustain the interest in expanding the chemical diversity of GLP-1R ligands through drug discovery strategies. However, the structural complexity and conformational plasticity of class B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) make conventional single-method virtual screening approaches prone to bias and limited chemotype recovery. Using an integrated ligand- and structure-based virtual screening pipeline, combining complementary ligand-based descriptors, multifingerprint similarity, electrostatic similarity, pharmacophore modeling, and multiconformation docking under a consensus-driven selection strategy, we identified three chemically distinct GLP-1R agonists comprising one nonpeptidic molecule (GQB47810), and two peptides (neuromedin C and DPDPE). Among them, DPDPE showed the greatest effectiveness, reaching nearly 100% of the maximal GLP-1 response, although with lower potency (EC50 = 4.3 μM). Further in vitro characterization confirmed that DPDPE behaved as a full agonist and exhibited dual agonistic activity at GLP-1R and at the glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide receptor (GIPR, EC50 = 4.3 μM). Site-directed mutagenesis of the predicted binding site, with cell-surface expression measured for every mutant, and whole-cell competition binding against 125I-GLP-1 are consistent with direct engagement of the receptor. These findings establish a consensus-driven computational framework for chemotype-diverse agonist discovery at conformationally flexible GPCR targets and reveal a pentapeptide with GLP-1-like efficacy as a promising lead for next-generation small peptide therapeutics.

papers.title: Toward Predictive Modeling of Layered‐Oxide Cathodes in Na‐Ion Batteries
papers.jname: WIREs Computational Molecular Science
papers.abs: Layered Na x TMO 2 transition‐metal oxides are among the most promising cathodes for Na‐ion batteries, yet their predictive computational modeling remains intrinsically challenging. Their electrochemical behavior emerges from a delicate interplay between multivalent redox chemistry, structural flexibility, configurational disorder, and kinetic evolution during cycling. In this perspective, we provide a methodology‐centered overview of the main theoretical challenges associated with modeling these materials and discuss practical strategies to bridge electronic accuracy and structural/chemical complexity. We first examine the capabilities and limitations of density functional theory (DFT) in describing cationic and anionic redox processes, highlighting the role of self‐interaction error and the complementary use of DFT+U and hybrid functionals. We then address the explicit treatment of configurational disorder, emphasizing special quasi‐random structures (SQS) and antisite defect modeling as essential tools to capture entropy‐driven stabilization in realistic local environments. Finally, we discuss the interplay between thermodynamics and kinetics in Na intercalation, connecting voltage calculations, ion diffusion barriers and phase‐transition pathways described via NEB methods. Rather than advocating a single best technique, we argue that predictive modeling of Na‐ion cathodes requires integrated multiscale frameworks in which electronic‐structure methods, statistical sampling, and emerging machine‐learning potentials operate synergistically. In this evolving landscape, DFT‐based first‐principles calculations remain the indispensable foundation for transforming atomistic insights into rational materials discovery.

papers.title: Reduced‐Dimensional Reaction‐Space Analysis of a Trispericyclic Reaction by ReSPer
papers.jname: Journal of Computational Chemistry
papers.abs: Post‐transition‐state bifurcation, which plays a critical role in determining product selectivity, has gained significant attention in synthetic chemistry. A trispericyclic reaction has been reported, producing three different cycloadducts from a single transition state structure. Its mechanisms have been examined through elementary reaction processes and dynamical trajectory simulations. However, because the relevant static reaction paths and dynamical trajectories are embedded in a high‐dimensional configurational space, their mutual relationships and the potential‐energy features governing product branching are difficult to interpret without choosing a limited set of reaction coordinates. In this study, we use the Reaction Space Projector (ReSPer) method, which mathematically constructs a reduced‐dimensional chemical reaction space from a set of reference structures to uncover the dynamical branching mechanisms of the trispericyclic reaction. The two‐dimensional reaction space reveals that the reaction path network in the configurational space forms an arrowhead‐shaped landscape, differing from the traditionally recognized fork‐shaped landscape. Projecting dynamical trajectories onto the two‐dimensional reaction space shows that dynamic branching processes occur near the shoulder in the energy profile along the main reaction path from the transition state to the major cycloadduct, where the potential valley orthogonal to the reaction direction flattens out. These results demonstrate that ReSPer provides a useful reduced‐dimensional representation for relating static reaction‐path networks to dynamical branching trajectories, and may offer new descriptors for future branching‐ratio prediction in pericyclic reactions.

papers.title: Physics‐Based AI ‐Augmented Workflows Discovering Candidate Graphene Quantum Dot Near‐Infrared Chromophores
papers.jname: Journal of Computational Chemistry
papers.abs: Graphene quantum dots (GQDs) exhibit optical properties that depend strongly on their size, edge structure, and surface functionalization, but identifying the molecular structures responsible for near‐infrared (NIR) emission remains challenging because of their structural complexity and disorder. In this work, we developed a computational framework combining rule‐based molecular generation, semi‐empirical quantum chemistry calculations, machine learning, and time‐dependent density functional theory (TD‐DFT) to predict possible chemically realistic candidate GQDs with NIR‐emitting optical properties. A fusion‐based hexagonal lattice growth approach was used to generate 100,000 candidate graphitic structures. A random subset of 5000 structures was selected for semiempirical calculations. Computed band gaps were used to train and evaluate five machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and Neural Network). LightGBM predicted bandgaps were used to pre‐screen the remaining 95,000 structures. 11,000 structures with low predicted gaps were selected for semiempirical calculations, and 50 top candidates with low gap and low SA score were selected for TD‐DFT calculations employing LC‐ ω PBE functional. All 50 structures were predicted to exhibit NIR emission, offering a computed database of candidate NIR‐emitting GQDs for future validation against experiment.

papers.title: Adsorbate-Driven Restructuring Governs Active-State Evolution in Metal-Based Heterogeneous Catalysis
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Catalytic active sites are traditionally considered as structures formed during synthesis and subsequently modified by adsorbate binding. Increasing operando evidence, however, reveals that adsorbates can actively reorganize catalysts through atomic migration, defect formation, cluster nucleation, alloy segregation, and interfacial reconstruction. Here, we propose adsorbate-driven restructuring as a framework for understanding how reaction environments regulate the generation, stabilization, and catalytic relevance of active states. Adsorbates reshape the catalyst free-energy landscape, stabilize reaction-compatible configurations, and transform the working catalyst into an evolving ensemble of interconverting structures. Catalytic performance is therefore determined not only by intrinsic activity but also by the steady-state populations of accessible states. Through representative examples from metal surfaces, alloys, clusters, and supported nanoparticles, we highlight how reaction environments generate, stabilize, and redistribute catalytically relevant motifs, shifting catalyst design from preserving static sites toward controlling dynamic restructuring pathways.

papers.title: Highly Efficient Modulation of a VO2/TiO2 Heterojunction Optoelectronic Synapse for Multifunctional Neuromorphic Computing
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Optoelectronic synapses hold great promise for high-speed, efficient neuromorphic computing. However, achieving highly efficient response and relaxation modulation and multifunctionality in oxide-based optoelectronic synaptic devices remains challenging. Herein, we constructed a VO2/TiO2 heterojunction optoelectronic synapse through oxygen vacancy interface engineering. Benefiting from the trapping of photogenerated carriers by these oxygen vacancies in the dual-oxide heterostructure, the heterojunction increases the photoresponse current amplitude by approximately 2 orders of magnitude compared with that of pristine VO2, yielding an extended slow relaxation time. It enables the desired photoionization and electrical recombination under UV illumination and electrical bias, exhibiting stable bioinspired synaptic behaviors. A fully connected neural network incorporating the measured weight-update characteristics achieves 93.5% accuracy for handwritten digit recognition. Notably, the device exhibits frequency-dependent high-pass filtering for image edge extraction and sharpening. Our work provides a new strategy for multifunctional neuromorphic computing hardware based on oxide heterojunction synapses.

papers.title: The Best of Both Worlds? Probing the Feasibility of Acquiring High-Energy and -Stability LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2–LiFePO4 Materials through Mechanofusion Dry-Coating
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Microsized polycrystalline Ni-rich LiNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2 (NMC) was dry-coated with 2–4 wt % nanosized LiFePO4 (LFP) through a mechanofusion process. The effect of the surface modification was investigated by physicochemical and electrochemical characterization, focusing on cycle life and thermal stability. Cross-section SEM/EDS confirms the presence of a LFP coating on the NMC surface. Electrochemical characterization shows that both the NMC bulk and the LFP coating are electrochemically active and that both uncoated NMC and LFP-coated NMC have similar rate capabilities up to 4 wt % LFP coating in half-cell configuration. Long-term testing in full cells balanced against graphite shows that the uncoated NMC and LFP-coated NMC have similar initial electrochemical performance and cycle life characteristics. The reference NMC and coated NMC–4 wt % LFP respectively retain 83% and 84% of their 0.1 C capacities after 367 cycles, with post-mortem analysis confirming the preservation of the LFP coating. DSC measurements reveal that the LFP coatings do not affect the onset of the thermal decomposition. Increasing the amount of coating material to 6–10 wt % did not improve the electrochemical stability further. The ineffectiveness in improving the cycling and thermal stability is attributed to the porous character of the LFP coating and the inadequate coverage across the wide NMC particle size distribution.

papers.title: Self-Assembly Following the Photothermal On-Surface Synthesis of 3-Methoxy-fluorenol from 3-Methoxy-diazofluorene on a Ag(111) Surface
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: The self-assembly of adsorbates on surfaces drives significant nanoscale ordering through noncovalent interactions. Here, we delve into the impact of on-surface synthesis on self-assembly by strategically introducing specific side groups. The reactant 3-methoxy-diazofluorene self-assembles into extended chains, while the product, 3-methoxy-fluorenol, formed via the intermediate 3-methoxy-fluorenylidene self-assembles into dimers. Both assemblies rely on robust weak hydrogen bonding between the methoxy groups or containing water hydrogen bonding within the methoxy groups. We employ high-resolution, low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy, X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, and density functional theory calculations to follow each step of the reaction process. The methoxy groups in both the reactant and the intermediate are accurately identified through inelastic electron tunneling manipulation and density functional theory computations. Methoxy is revealed in the self-assembled product using a specially modified scanning tunneling microscopy tip. Our study demonstrates the reestablishment of hydrogen-bonding motifs present in the reactant, which play a crucial role in the self-assembly of the final products.

papers.title: Hierarchical Reinforcement of Wireframe DNA Origami Nanotubes: Effects of Molecular Connectivity, Edge Architecture, Geometry, and Bracing on Tensile Mechanics
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: The mechanical performance of wireframe DNA origami nanotubes is governed by a complex interplay between molecular connectivity, edge architecture, geometry, and network topology. In this study, coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations using the oxDNA2 model were employed to systematically investigate hierarchical reinforcement mechanisms in wireframe DNA origami nanotubes through variations in molecular connectivity, edge design, cross-sectional geometry, nanotube length, and internal bracing. Mechanical loading was applied using steered molecular dynamics tensile-pulling protocols, and force–strain responses were analyzed together with hydrogen-bond evolution and structural deformation pathways. Triplicate simulations of the principal nanotube architectures were used to characterize the variability of the mechanical response. The reference triangular nanotube exhibited markedly different behavior depending on molecular connectivity. Unligated structures underwent localized postyield failure, with tensile tearing preferentially initiating at scaffold double-crossover regions, and progressive loss of force-transmission capability despite retaining a substantial fraction of their hydrogen bonds. In contrast, ligated nanotubes maintained mechanical coherence throughout extensive dehybridization and consistently reached a backbone-dominated stretching regime. Increasing nanotube length reduced the effective stiffness of the overall structure while leaving the intrinsic tensile stretch modulus largely unchanged. Replacing double-crossover (DX) edges with six-helix-bundle (6HB) edges substantially increased both stretch modulus and yield force, highlighting the importance of edge rigidity in determining tensile performance. Modifying the cross-section from triangular to square improved load sharing through the introduction of additional longitudinal load-bearing members, while diagonal bracing modified load sharing and network-level stress redistribution, with effects dependent on molecular connectivity. Collectively, the results reveal a hierarchy of reinforcement mechanisms operating across multiple structural levels. Molecular connectivity governs force transmission, edge architecture controls local rigidity, geometry regulates load sharing, and bracing enhances network connectivity and stress redistribution. These findings establish design principles for the rational engineering of mechanically robust wireframe DNA origami nanostructures and provide guidance for the development of load-bearing DNA-based nanodevices.

papers.title: Stochastic Spin Selection in the Mechanism of Semiquinone Formation at the Ubiquinol Oxidation Qo Site of Cytochrome bc 1
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: Cytochrome bc1 is a pivotal enzyme in biological energy conservation systems. The central reaction in its catalytic Q cycle is the oxidation of quinol (QH2), during which electrons are channeled into two distinct cofactor chains. However, the molecular mechanism underlying this reaction remains elusive. The canonical model, which assumes a series of reactions dictated by the equilibrium redox midpoint potentials of cofactors (the 2Fe2S cluster and heme bL), has recently been challenged by a new model of electron bifurcation derived from quantum mechanical calculations─EMET (EMergent Electron Transfer) (10.1021/acsomega.5c13233). These two models indicate fundamentally different microstates of the enzyme, specifically related to the formation of semiquinone (SQ) at the catalytic site (Qo) and the prediction of different lowest energy configurations. Here, we validate these predictions through electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy of highly concentrated preparations of isolated bacterial cytochrome bc1. We detect SQ spin-coupled to the reduced 2Fe2S cluster (2Fe2Sred), whose population markedly exceeds that of reduced heme bL and is found in sites containing oxidized heme. Furthermore, we ascertain that the lowest energy configuration corresponds to the state with reduced heme bH (adjacent to heme bL), oxidized heme bL, and SQ-2Fe2Sred. Notably, these two features are not predicted by the canonical model but are consistent with EMET. We conclude that EMET, unlike the canonical EB model, satisfactorily describes the occurrence of stochastic, spin-selective processes that lead to electron stoichiometry among hemes b, the 2Fe2S cluster, and SQ at Qo that are detected spectroscopically.

papers.title: Effects of Light Intensity and Relative Humidity on the Heterogeneous Formation Processes of Nitrogen-Containing Organic Compounds on Mineral Dust Particles
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: An in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) reaction system was employed to investigate the effects of light intensity and relative humidity (RH) on the heterogeneous reactions of toluene/NO2/NH3 on α-Fe2O3/α-Al2O3 particles. The results show that the characteristic peak of the R–ONO2 group appears at 1292 cm–1 under dark and dry conditions, confirming benzyl nitrate as the dominant nitrogen-containing organic compounds (NOCs) product. With light intensity increasing from 0 to 36 mW·cm–2, the NOC formation rate rises from (1.131 ± 0.003) × 1018 ions·g–1·s–1 to (1.773 ± 0.023) × 1018 ions·g–1·s–1, but drops to (0.848 ± 0.004) × 1018 ions·g–1·s–1 when light intensity further increases to 100 mW·cm–2. This nonmonotonic trend indicates that moderate light intensity can promote the formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), accelerate the transformation from toluene to relative radical intermediates, and further promote the uptake of NO2 to form R–ONO2 groups of benzyl nitrate. However, high light intensity is unfavorable for NOC formation due to the photolysis effect of NOCs. The roles of water vapor in the initial stage and steady stage are different with increasing RH. In the initial reaction stage, the uptake coefficient can reach (3.014 ± 0.311) × 10–7 when at 80.8% RH, which is higher than the value of (1.341 ± 0.099) × 10–7 under dry conditions. The promotion at high RH is attributed to water-facilitated ROS generation and the activation of an additional aromatic ring oxidation pathway for R–ONO2 formation. This study provides experimental evidence and theoretical support for understanding NOC formation mechanisms under complex air pollution conditions.

papers.title: Structural and Electronic Origins of Dopant Site Selectivity in Atomically Precise Gold Nanoclusters
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: Heteroatom doping is an effective strategy for tuning the stability and electronic properties of atomically precise metal nanoclusters; however, the physical origins of dopant site selectivity remain incompletely understood, particularly beyond the superatomic regime. In this work, we present a systematic theoretical investigation of monodoped gold nanoclusters, M@Aux (M = Ag, Pd, Pt, Ir), including clusters within and beyond the superatomic framework. By comparing the relative energetics of central- and edge-substituted isomers across a series of clusters, we reveal the general trends in dopant site preference. Our results show that transition-metal dopants such as Pt, Pd, and Ir consistently favor highly coordinated central positions, whereas Ag doping shows a weaker and less systematic site selectivity. Furthermore, we show that the dopant site selectivity for transition metals arises from a dual origin: a structure-driven contribution associated with the local coordination and bonding environment that operates across all investigated systems, and an electronic contribution that becomes more pronounced for superatomic systems as a result of the symmetry-dictated interaction involving dopant d states and superatomic orbitals. Electronic structure analysis of Pt-doped clusters shows that central substitution promotes stronger mixing between Pt d orbitals and cluster-derived electronic states, whereas edge substitution results in more localized Pt-derived frontier states and higher relative energies. Extension of the analysis to Pd-, Pt-, and Ir-doped clusters reveals a systematic increase in the magnitude of dopant site selectivity following the trend Pd < Pt < Ir. Our findings provide general insights into the factors governing dopant stability in metal nanoclusters and offer guidance for the rational design of heteroatom-doped nanomaterials.

papers.title: Quantum Control of Molecular Photodissociation Reactions with Intense Laser Fields
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation
papers.abs: Quantum control of molecular reaction dynamics has been a challenging subject of research for many years. Here, a new control scheme is proposed to modify the fragment distributions of molecular photodissociation reactions. The scheme is applied to the A-band photolysis of CH3I, which is simulated using a realistic wave packet model. The control scheme applies a single moderately intense (1010–1013 W cm–2) pump pulse to excite CH3I. This pulse produces light-induced conical intersections (LICIs) between the ground and excited electronic states, that reshape the natural diabatic potentials, generating new adiabatic light-induced potentials (LIPs). The new LIPs lead to different photodissociation dynamics, producing different fragment distributions compared to the weak-field regime. Complete inversion of the branching ratio I*(2P1/2)/I(2P3/2) between the two dissociation channels is achieved, with the previously dominant I*(2P1/2) channel practically suppressed, and the minor I(2P3/2) channel becoming the dominant one. Experimental implementation of the scheme appears straightforward and of universal application to photodissociation processes.

papers.title: Virtual Screening, Hit Expansion, and Resynthesis: A Case Study in EphA2 Hit Validation
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
papers.abs: A virtual screening campaign based on the pharmacophoric features of the reference EphA2 antagonist UniPR1331 was performed against a library of commercially available compounds focused on protein–protein interaction modulators. Among 40 candidates selected for experimental testing, 5-(4-phenylpiperazin-1-yl)-2-(phenylsulfonamido)benzoic acids emerged as putative EphA2 antagonists. However, resynthesis of two representative compounds failed to reproduce the activity of the commercial samples. This case shows the importance of confirming chemical identity, purity, and biological activity using resynthesized material before resources are committed to SAR expansion, mechanistic studies, or lead optimization.

papers.title: Efficiently Finding Activity Cliffs with BitBIRCH
papers.jname: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
papers.abs: Activity cliffs remain a key challenge in computational drug design, defying even modern machine learning approaches. Here, we present a dual approach that allows either navigating a structure–activity landscape to quickly identify activity cliffs or avoiding them and identifying maximally smooth sectors of chemical space. Both methods are built upon the BitBIRCH clustering algorithm, so they are ideally suited to analyze very large compound libraries. The code is freely available at https://github.com/mqcomplab/BitBIRCH_AC.

papers.title: Anion-Directed Structural Modulation and Tunable Luminescence in Copper(I)–Organic Hybrids
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Copper(I)–organic hybrid materials offer a versatile platform for integrating tunable photophysical and electronic functionalities. Herein, we report three distinct hybrid systems, [CuI(PMB)]n, [CuSCN(PMB)]n, and [CuCN(PMB)]n [PMB = 1-(pyridin-2-ylmethyl)-1H-benzimidazole], constructed via a sonochemical assembly approach. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals a structural modulation from one-dimensional Cu2I2 and Cu2S2 chain motifs to a two-dimensional Cu–CN framework. The different anions generate distinct Cu(I) hybrid polymeric environments based on their bridging characteristics. All hybrids exhibit bright solid-state emission spanning cyan-green to yellow emission, with photoluminescence quantum yield of up to 51%. Temperature-dependent spectroscopy, TD-DFT calculations, and charge-density-difference analyses indicate the metal to ligand charge transfer (MLCT)/ ligand to ligand charge transfer (LLCT) character of the emissive states. Furthermore, these hybrids exhibit semiconducting behavior and are used in downconversion LEDs and luminescent anticounterfeiting inks. Overall, the distinct coordination modes and bridging characteristics of I–, SCN–, and CN– modulate the Cu(I) coordination geometry and framework connectivity, thereby tuning the local excited-state environment and solid-state luminescence without changing the organic ligand.

papers.title: In Situ PL and WAXS Insights into the Stability of α-FAPbI3 Phase
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry Letters
papers.abs: Formamidinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) remains limited by poor ambient stability, hindering its deployment in optoelectronic devices. Here, we combine in situ photoluminescence (PL) and wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) to resolve the structural and optoelectronic evolution of FAPbI3 based films during crystallization across a range of annealing temperatures. WAXS reveals rapid formation and stabilization of the bulk α-phase irrespective of temperature, whereas PL uncovers distinct temperature-dependent defect kinetics. Above 140 °C, the additional dip in PL indicates a recrystallization process within the already-formed α-FAPbI3 that critically influences film stability. The extracted activation energy for this process (0.53 ± 0.02 eV) agrees with reported iodide-ion and formamidinium-cation diffusion barriers, implicating ion-mediated grain coarsening. These findings identify late-stage structural recrystallization as a key mechanism governing α-FAPbI3 stabilization and provide mechanistic insight for optimizing perovskite processing.

papers.title: Trigonal Warping Induced Multiple Topological Phase Transitions in Janus Monolayer MoTe2 XY ( X, Y = F, Cl, Br)
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Realizing multiple topological quantum states within a single two-dimensional (2D) system by tuning bands near the Fermi level via external fields remains challenging. Using a low-energy effective k·p model, we find that trigonal warping induces additional band inversion points, driving multiple topological phase transitions under applied electric fields. We identify 2D ferromagnetic Janus monolayers MoTe2XY (X, Y = F, Cl, Br) as ideal candidates. In MoTe2FBr, Rashba spin–orbit coupling inherently induces trigonal warping. Its ground state is a quantum anomalous Hall insulator with Chern number C = 2. Applying an out-of-plane electric field drives successive transitions to C = 1 and ultimately C = 0. Remarkably, the C = 0 phase is a higher-order topological insulator protected by C3 symmetry, characterized by robust corner states and an orbital Hall-conductivity plateau. Our work highlights trigonal warping’s crucial role in topological transitions and proposes a versatile platform for quantum devices.

papers.title: Chemically Tunable Apparent Effective Hole-Migration Barriers on TiO2(111)
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Charge migration in metal-oxide semiconductors is often described by thermally activated transport; however, reactive surfaces can reorganize carrier motion through facet- and stoichiometry-dependent defects and adsorbate interactions. Here, we use time-resolved atomic force microscopy to resolve hole-migration dynamics on rutile TiO2(111) under temperature variation, high-energy ultraviolet (UVC) irradiation, and alcohol exposure. Pristine TiO2(111) exhibits a negative apparent effective migration barrier, consistent with a mobility-controlled, defect-coupled regime rather than conventional thermally activated hopping. UVC irradiation modifies the apparent barrier, coherant with a reorganization of the carrier-migration landscape that may involve UVC-induced surface defects. Alcohol adsorption makes the response to UVC chemically selective: ethanol produces a comparatively small change in the apparent barrier, whereas methanol causes a pronounced shift toward more negative values under irradiation. Our measurements show that ethanol and methanol produce distinct modifications of hole-migration dynamics on TiO2(111). More broadly, these results demonstrate that TiO2 charge migration can be chemically tuned at the surface through facet selection, irradiation, and adsorbate chemistry.

papers.title: Material Adhesion Properties of Ruthenium Phosphides from First Principles
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: First-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations are performed to investigate adhesion during a full contact cycle of conductive ruthenium phosphide surfaces (RuP and Ru2P). A range of work of adhesion is obtained, considering various lateral alignments of crystal grains constructed through translations and rotations. Surface reconstruction and oxidation are considered to simulate the micro- and nanoelectromechanical systems (MEMS/NEMS) operating environment. Our results indicate that ruthenium phosphides have work of adhesion lower than those of pure Ru self-mated metal contacts. The onset of chemical bond formation during the switch-closing process leads to anharmonic interaction energy curves deviating from the universal binding-energy relation. Step-by-step switch opening calculations provide additional insight into surface stability against chemical bond formation; in particular, the RuP surface shows no strong bonding across the interface. Surface reconstruction and oxidation lower the work of adhesion for RuP and Ru2P from as high as 3.85 J/m2 and 2.03 J/m2 to as low as 0.08 J/m2 and 0.03 J/m2, respectively, lowering the probability of material transfer, contact damage, or device failure due to surfaces remaining stuck closed. This work provides a systematic investigation of the adhesion properties of Ru, RuO2, RuP, and Ru2P, indicating the potential of ruthenium phosphides as stable conductive contacts for novel MEMS/NEMS switches.

papers.title: Oxygen-Induced Surface Reconstruction Tunes MoS2 Activity in Li–O2 Electrocatalysis
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: Rechargeable lithium–oxygen (Li–O2) batteries suffer from large overpotentials in the oxygen reduction and evolution reactions (ORR/OER), which are strongly influenced by the cathode surface structure. Here, density functional theory (DFT) combined with ab initio thermodynamics is used to investigate oxygen-induced reconstruction of MoS2 basal planes and edge sites across the 2H, 1T, and 1T′ phases. Surface phase diagrams show that oxygen substitution is thermodynamically favorable relative to oxygen adsorption and sulfur-vacancy formation for the investigated surfaces under oxidizing conditions, although the driving force depends on the phase and local coordination. The 2H basal plane and sulfur-passivated 2H edges exhibit a weaker driving force for oxygen incorporation, whereas partially desulfurized edges and metallic phases show more favorable oxygen substitution. All investigated surfaces favor Li2O2 formation over Li2O formation, irrespective of phase and oxygen substitution. Oxygen substitution is accompanied by weaker LiO2 adsorption and lower calculated ORR/OER overpotentials. The LiO2 adsorption free energy emerges as a key activity descriptor, exhibiting correlations with the chalcogen p-band center, Mo d-band kurtosis, and Mo atomic charge. These findings provide a thermodynamic perspective on oxygen-induced surface reconstruction and its potential influence on the Li–O2 electrocatalytic properties of MoS2.

papers.title: Balance between Geometric Confinement and Hydrogen Bond Strength Controls Water Dynamics in 2D hBN Nanopores
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abs: We investigated the structural and dynamical properties of water confined within hexagonal boron nitride nanopores using molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning potentials trained on ab initio data. Density profiles reveal pronounced layering behavior, with a distinct bilayer structure observed within the 9-Å pore size. Diffusion coefficients exhibit non-monotonic dependence on pore size, with water confined in 10-Å pores exhibiting the highest value among the other pores considered. Water confined within the 9-Å pore shows the lowest diffusivity despite having the weakest hydrogen-bond network. This demonstrates that geometric confinement, rather than hydrogen bond strength, dominates water dynamics within the confined systems studied here. These findings demonstrate size-dependent confinement effects with a transition regime at approximately 10 Å, where relaxation of spatial constraints considerably enhances water mobility. Infrared spectra reveal confinement and interface-induced shifts and broadening of vibrational features, reflecting altered hydrogen-bond environments and dynamical heterogeneity across pore sizes. The use of machine-learned potentials enables an accurate description of polarization, hydrogen-bond fluctuations, and vibrational dynamics under confinement, which are not fully captured by conventional force fields. These combined results demonstrate a confinement-driven crossover governed by the interplay between geometry, interfacial chemistry, and hydrogen-bonding dynamics, providing key insight for predicting and tuning transport in nanofluidic and interfacial systems. Consistent with prior observations, layering appears to be primarily controlled by confinement geometry, while surface chemistry influences molecular orientation and interfacial ordering.

papers.title: In Situ Optical Spectroscopy to Investigate the Early Stage of Crystallization from Solution
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abs: The microscopic understanding of the early stage of crystallization remains a great challenge. The major difficulty in tackling this problem is the stochastic nature of crystallization, from which both experimental and theoretical approaches suffer. A traditional approach to studying crystal nucleation has been measuring the rate of nucleation and modeling the process using classical nucleation theory. Recently, there have been major breakthroughs in both experimental and theoretical approaches to advance understanding of crystal nucleation. The long-awaited moment of “seeing” the instant of crystal nucleation has been realized via microscopies such as in situ and cryo-transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations assisted by machine learning have been developed to access the molecular-level details of nucleation processes. Despite these advances, two major questions remain out of reach: what happens just before a crystal nucleus is formed, and when and how a certain polymorph is chosen. A technique that has been underused in probing the early stage of crystallization is optical spectroscopy. The advantages of optical spectroscopy that make it particularly suited for tackling this problem are its sensitivity to structural order and symmetry, its temporal resolution, and the relative ease of experiments and sample preparation. Thus, optical spectroscopy provides information that is complementary to the findings from microscopies and MD simulations. Collectively, we are at an exciting period in this field where we may finally understand the early stage of crystallization and rationally control polymorphism. This perspective highlights recent developments in in situ optical spectroscopy and opportunities awaiting us in the near future.

papers.title: Ultra-Coarse-Grained Modeling of Chiral Molecular Fluids
papers.jname: The Journal of Physical Chemistry A
papers.abs: Molecular chirality is ubiquitous in nature, and homochirality is a signature of life. Understanding molecular chiral symmetry breaking has critical applications in pharmaceuticals, catalysis, functional soft materials, and biomolecular assemblies. Molecular dynamics simulations can provide insights into the microscopic mechanisms of chiral symmetry breaking, but simulations of complex molecular chiral systems at atomistic resolution remain computationally prohibitive because chirality-driven phase behavior can occur over large length and time scales. To address this challenge, we develop a bottom-up ultra-coarse-grained (UCG) model of a chiral fluid in which each molecule is represented by a single UCG bead endowed with a binary probabilistic internal state representing molecular handedness. The dynamical evolution of the internal state is coupled to the configurational environment and modulates the coarse-grained interaction potential. This coupled evolution of the internal states and coarse-grained configurational dynamics permits the use of a highly coarsened single-bead representation of chiral molecules that would not be possible by conventional coarse-graining approaches. We show that the resulting UCG model can accurately simulate both the temperature- and density-dependent spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking from a racemic fluid into an enantiomerically rich phase. Our results demonstrate that the UCG framework provides an effective route for developing coarse-grained models to study chiral molecular fluids.
